articles.title: How Do You Validate `unknown` in TypeScript Without a Schema Library? 🛡️

articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who is obsessed with gamba. 😸🦐

Recently, I was thinking about a very common TypeScript problem.

Suppose some value comes from:

  • an API response
  • JSON.parse
  • local storage
  • a message payload
  • third-party code

What type should it have before we actually verify it?

Probably this

declare const input: unknown;

That part is easy.

The interesting question is what comes next.

How do we safely turn that unknown into something useful?

And do we really need a full schema library every time?

Let's look at it! 👀

Validate unknown in TypeScript Without a Schema Library | is-kit

Validate unknown TypeScript values with small composable type guards and safeParse, without adopting a schema-first validation workflow.

is-kit.dev

🧱 unknown Is Doing Its Job

Suppose we have

declare const input: unknown;

input.name;
// Error

TypeScript refuses to let us access name.

At first this can feel annoying.

But TypeScript is actually telling us something important

We have a value.

We do not know what it is yet.

That is exactly what an untrusted boundary value should mean.

An HTTP response does not become a User just because our application expects a User.

Neither does parsed JSON.

So I like to think of unknown like this

unknown is not missing type information.

It is an honest description of a value we have not verified yet.

The problem is not unknown.

The problem is how we establish trust.

😈 The Easy Escape: as User

There is a very short way out.

type User = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
};

declare const input: unknown;

const user = input as User;

user.name.toUpperCase();

TypeScript is happy.

Nice! 🎉

Except, nothing was actually checked.

This still works

const input = {
  id: "user-1",
  name: 123,
} as unknown;

const user = input as User;

user.name.toUpperCase();
// 💥 Runtime error

as User changes what the compiler believes.

It does not inspect the runtime value.
It does not add missing properties.
It does not turn 123 into a string.

So if runtime trust matters, a type assertion is not validation.

We need an actual runtime check.

🛡️ A Type Guard Connects Runtime and TypeScript

Let's start small.

With is-kit, we can build a guard like this

import { isString, oneOfValues, struct } from "is-kit";

const isUser = struct({
  id: isString,
  name: isString,
  role: oneOfValues("admin", "member"),
});

Now we can pass unknown directly to it

declare const input: unknown;

if (isUser(input)) {
  input.name.toUpperCase();

  // input:
  // Readonly<{
  //   id: string;
  //   name: string;
  //   role: "admin" | "member";
  // }>
}

This is the part I like.

The same check does two jobs

runtime
→ does this value actually match?

TypeScript
→ what is this value after the check succeeds?

There is no separate schema definition and no type assertion.

We just compose small runtime predicates.

🧩 The Shape Can Grow Naturally

Real payloads are usually a little more complicated.

Maybe a user has:

  • an optional profile
  • a nullable bio
  • a list of tags

We can keep composing guards

import {
  arrayOf,
  isString,
  nullable,
  oneOfValues,
  optionalKey,
  struct,
} from "is-kit";

const isProfile = struct({
  displayName: isString,
  bio: optionalKey(nullable(isString)),
});

const isUser = struct({
  id: isString,
  role: oneOfValues("admin", "member"),
  profile: optionalKey(isProfile),
  tags: arrayOf(isString),
});

Then

isUser({
  id: "user-1",
  role: "member",
  tags: ["typescript", "guards"],
});
// true

But

isUser({
  id: "user-1",
  role: "owner",
  tags: ["typescript"],
});
// false

Each piece is still just a guard.

That means we can test it independently, reuse it somewhere else, or compose it into something larger.

There is also an important difference here

optionalKey(...)

means

the property may be absent

while

nullable(...)

means

the value may be null

Those are different runtime contracts, so I prefer keeping them separate.

📦 What Does safeParse Add?

A direct guard is often enough.

if (isUser(input)) {
  renderUser(input);
}

But sometimes I want the validation result itself to move through the program.

For example

const result = safeParse(isUser, input);

if (!result.valid) {
  return { status: 400 as const };
}

return {
  status: 200 as const,
  user: result.value,
};

safeParse gives us a small tagged result

{
  valid: (true, value);
}

or

{
  valid: false;
}

So TypeScript can narrow it with a normal branch.

The important part is what safeParse does not do.

It does not:

  • clone the value
  • coerce the value
  • generate a new object
  • transform invalid data into valid data

On success, it returns the same value after the guard has accepted it.

So I think of the difference like this

guard
→ boolean + narrowing

safeParse
→ tagged result + validated value

Same runtime rule.

Different control-flow shape.

🧃 What About JSON?

This is one of the most common boundaries.

const value = JSON.parse(body);

The awkward part is that JSON.parse returns any.

So now the unsafe value can spread through the program before we validate it.

Instead, we can keep the boundary small

import { safeJsonParse } from "is-kit";

declare const body: string;

const result = safeJsonParse(body, isUser);

if (!result.valid) {
  return { status: 400 as const };
}

renderUser(result.value);

Conceptually, the flow is

JSON text
   ↓
decode
   ↓
unknown
   ↓
guard
   ↓
validated value

Invalid JSON and guard failures both produce

{
  valid: false;
}

And again, nothing is coerced just to make the value pass.

I like this because the unsafe part stays right at the decode boundary.

🚪 Should Extra Keys Be Allowed?

There is another small design choice that appears at object boundaries.

Suppose we expect

{
  username: string;
  password: string;
}

Should this also be accepted?

{
  username: "Neko",
  password: "secret",
  admin: true,
}

With struct, extra keys are allowed by default.

That is often useful for API responses because a server may add a new field without breaking an older client.

But sometimes we really want a closed object shape.

Then we can use

const isCredentials = struct(
  {
    username: isString,
    password: isString,
  },
  { exact: true },
);

Now

isCredentials({
  username: "Neko",
  password: "secret",
});
// true

while

isCredentials({
  username: "Neko",
  password: "secret",
  admin: true,
});
// false

The important part is not that one mode is always better.

It is that the boundary should express the contract we actually want.

🤔 So Do We Still Need Schema Libraries?

Yes.

Sometimes absolutely.

A type guard toolkit and a schema library overlap a little, but they are not trying to solve exactly the same problem.

For example, a schema library is probably the better choice when we need:

  • structured validation errors with field paths
  • multiple validation issues at once
  • coercion
  • default values
  • transformations
  • schema-generated types or external artifacts
  • deep integration with a form or API framework

Those are larger validation workflows.

is-kit asks a narrower question

Does this value satisfy this runtime predicate?

If yes, what can TypeScript safely narrow it to?

That narrower model is sometimes exactly what I want.

For example

Approach Good fit
Inline typeof checks One small local condition
Type guards Reusable boolean validation and narrowing
Schema library Rich validation, transformation, and schema workflows

So I don't think the question is

Type guards or schema libraries—which one wins?

The more useful question is

What is the smallest validation model that solves this boundary?

🎯 The Important Part

I started with a simple value

declare const input: unknown;

The tempting shortcut was

const user = input as User;

But that only changes TypeScript's belief.

It does not establish runtime trust.

A runtime guard gives us a much more useful flow

unknown
   ↓
runtime check
   ↓
narrowed value

And when we want a result-oriented API

unknown
   ↓
guard
   ↓
safeParse
   ↓
{ valid: true, value }
or
{ valid: false }

No hidden conversion.

No assertion pretending the check already happened.

Just small runtime rules that TypeScript can understand too. 😸

articles.title: TypeScript `ReadonlyMap` and `ReadonlySet` in 2026: Immutable Collections That Stop Accidental Mutation at the Type Level
articles.description: Learn how TypeScript's ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet prevent accidental mutations at compile time, when to use them over Record and Map, and how to build type-safe cache APIs and configuration systems that enforce immutability.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet in 2026: Immutable Collections That Stop Accidental Mutation at the Type Level

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Why ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet Matter in 2026

Most runtime bugs in TypeScript codebases stem from unintended mutation of shared data structures. A cache gets modified during a read operation. A configuration set changes after initialization. A lookup map loses entries when a function meant to query it accidentally calls .delete(). The type system allows these mutations because developers reach for Map and Set everywhere, even when the collection should never change after construction.

The solution exists at the type level. ReadonlyMap<K, V> and ReadonlySet<T> strip mutating methods from the interface, making accidental writes a compile-time error instead of a production incident. Teams that adopt these types as the default for exposed collections catch entire classes of bugs before code review.

Problem flow showing accidental mutation passing type check

The correct pattern flips this. Return ReadonlyMap from any function that provides a view into shared state. The compiler blocks mutation attempts immediately, and the intent becomes explicit in the signature.

Solution flow showing compile-time prevention

This matters because the cost of a production cache corruption or a silently modified feature flag set is orders of magnitude higher than the friction of adding readonly to a type annotation. The pattern scales: once teams default to readonly collections, mutation becomes an explicit opt-in, and the codebase self-documents which functions preserve state versus transform it.

Key Takeaways

  • ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet remove mutating methods at the type level, preventing accidental writes to shared collections.
  • Returning readonly collections from functions makes immutability explicit in the signature and catches bugs at compile time.
  • The type-level protection has zero runtime cost but does not prevent mutation if the underlying reference is cast back to a mutable type.
  • Use ReadonlyMap for cache APIs and lookup tables; use ReadonlySet for configuration flags and whitelists that initialize once.
  • Runtime immutability requires defensive copies or immutable data structure libraries; TypeScript's readonly is a compile-time guard only.

The Type-Level Contract: What Readonly Actually Enforces

ReadonlyMap<K, V> is a type that omits .set(), .delete(), and .clear() from the Map interface. A function that receives a ReadonlyMap can call .get(), .has(), .keys(), .values(), .entries(), and .forEach(), but any attempt to mutate the collection fails at compile time.

The compiler enforces this contract through structural typing. When a function signature declares a ReadonlyMap parameter, TypeScript checks that the argument provides the readonly methods and lacks the mutating ones. This happens at the type level only. At runtime, a ReadonlyMap is still a Map instance. The protection disappears if the value is cast back to Map or if JavaScript code bypasses the type system.

Type-level contract hierarchy

The same structure applies to ReadonlySet<T>. It omits .add(), .delete(), and .clear() but retains .has(), .size, .keys(), .values(), .entries(), and .forEach(). The type system prevents mutation wherever the readonly variant appears.

This distinction is critical. The readonly types are not runtime wrappers or proxies. They are compile-time views that restrict the available operations. A Map can be passed where a ReadonlyMap is expected because it satisfies the readonly interface (it has all the read methods). The reverse does not hold: a ReadonlyMap cannot be passed where a Map is expected because it lacks the mutation methods.

The practical consequence is that functions should accept the narrowest type that supports their operations. If a function only queries a map, its parameter should be ReadonlyMap. If it must mutate the map, the parameter must be Map. The signature communicates intent, and the compiler enforces it.

Building Immutable Cache APIs with ReadonlyMap

A cache that exposes a mutable Map invites accidental corruption. The correct pattern returns a ReadonlyMap view while maintaining a private mutable instance for internal updates.

class UserCache {
  private cache = new Map<string, User>();

  set(id: string, user: User): void {
    this.cache.set(id, user);
  }

  getAll(): ReadonlyMap<string, User> {
    return this.cache;
  }

  get(id: string): User | undefined {
    return this.cache.get(id);
  }

  clear(): void {
    this.cache.clear();
  }
}

const cache = new UserCache();
cache.set("u1", { id: "u1", name: "Alice" });

const snapshot = cache.getAll();
// snapshot.set("u2", { id: "u2", name: "Bob" }); // Compiler error
// snapshot.delete("u1"); // Compiler error
const user = snapshot.get("u1"); // Works

The getAll() method returns the internal map typed as ReadonlyMap. No defensive copy is needed because the type system prevents external mutation. The cache controls when writes happen through explicit methods like .set() and .clear(). Consumers receive a view that guarantees the cache state will not change underneath their logic.

This pattern extends to more complex scenarios. A query result cache that aggregates data from multiple sources can return a readonly snapshot. A configuration loader that reads from a file can expose the parsed values as a ReadonlyMap, ensuring that application code cannot accidentally overwrite settings.

Cache API returning ReadonlyMap for safe external access

The failure mode here is subtle but expensive. If getAll() returned Map<string, User>, a caller could write cache.getAll().clear(), wiping the entire cache without triggering a type error. The bug might surface minutes or hours later when a lookup fails. The readonly return type makes this impossible at compile time.

The tradeoff is that consumers must explicitly call mutating methods on the cache instance itself. Code that needs to modify the cache cannot do so through the snapshot. This friction is the design goal: mutation becomes an intentional action on a controlled API surface.

ReadonlySet for Configuration and Feature Flags

Feature flags and configuration whitelists initialize once and should never change during the application lifecycle. A ReadonlySet enforces this constraint at the type level.

class FeatureFlags {
  private flags: Set<string>;

  constructor(enabledFlags: string[]) {
    this.flags = new Set(enabledFlags);
  }

  getEnabled(): ReadonlySet<string> {
    return this.flags;
  }

  isEnabled(flag: string): boolean {
    return this.flags.has(flag);
  }
}

const features = new FeatureFlags(["beta-ui", "analytics-v2"]);
const enabled = features.getEnabled();

if (enabled.has("beta-ui")) {
  // Render new UI
}

// enabled.add("experimental-mode"); // Compiler error
// enabled.delete("analytics-v2"); // Compiler error

The getEnabled() method returns a ReadonlySet view. Application code can check membership but cannot add or remove flags. Changes to the feature set require restarting the application or reloading configuration through a controlled mechanism.

Feature flag system flow with readonly enforcement

This pattern applies to any configuration that loads once and stays constant. A whitelist of allowed origins for CORS. A set of valid API versions. A registry of registered plugin names. The readonly return type communicates that these values are fixed after initialization.

The alternative is to return Set and trust that callers will not mutate it. That trust breaks when a developer unfamiliar with the system writes features.getEnabled().add() in a new feature branch. The type system catches this immediately if the signature returns ReadonlySet.

The same principle extends to more complex configuration objects. A settings object can use ReadonlyMap<string, ConfigValue> to expose parsed values while keeping the underlying map private. The type system prevents accidental overwrites of critical settings like database URLs or API keys.

ReadonlyMap vs Record vs Map: Choosing the Right Structure

Three structures store key-value pairs in TypeScript: Map, Record, and ReadonlyMap. Each has a distinct use case.

Use Map when keys are not known at compile time and mutation is required. A cache that adds entries dynamically. A dependency graph that builds incrementally. The structure needs .set(), .delete(), and .clear().

Use Record<K, V> when keys are known at compile time and the structure is a plain object. Configuration parsed from JSON. An enum-to-metadata lookup. The values are fixed or updated through object spread. Records benefit from exact property checking and do not require runtime Map instantiation.

Use ReadonlyMap when exposing a view of a mutable map that external code should not modify. Cache snapshots. Query result lookups. The structure provides efficient iteration and membership tests without risking accidental mutation.

Comparison of Map, Record, and ReadonlyMap use cases

The performance characteristics differ. Map uses hashing for lookups and insertion. Record uses property access, which V8 optimizes aggressively for objects with fixed shapes. ReadonlyMap has the same performance as Map because it is a Map at runtime. The type annotation has no runtime cost.

The immutability guarantee also differs. Record types are mutable by default unless marked with Readonly<Record<K, V>>. Even then, TypeScript's Readonly only makes top-level properties readonly. Nested objects remain mutable. ReadonlyMap is a shallow constraint: the map itself cannot be mutated, but the values it holds can be if they are mutable types.

The implication here is that ReadonlyMap<string, User[]> prevents adding or removing entries, but it does not prevent pushing elements into the arrays stored as values. If deep immutability is required, the value type must also be readonly: ReadonlyMap<string, readonly User[]>.

This tradeoff matters in practice. A cache returning ReadonlyMap<string, MutableObject> prevents callers from replacing entire entries but allows modification of the objects themselves. If that is unacceptable, the cache must return defensive copies or use an immutable data structure library.

Runtime Immutability: When TypeScript's readonly Isn't Enough

TypeScript's readonly modifier and ReadonlyMap are compile-time constructs. They do not enforce immutability at runtime. A value typed as ReadonlyMap can be cast to Map with as Map, bypassing the readonly constraint entirely. JavaScript code that interacts with TypeScript modules sees only runtime maps with no readonly protection.

function dangerousOperation(cache: ReadonlyMap<string, number>): void {
  // Type assertion removes compile-time protection
  const mutableCache = cache as Map<string, number>;
  mutableCache.set("attack", 999);
}

const cache = new Map<string, number>([["key", 1]]);
dangerousOperation(cache);
console.log(cache.get("attack")); // 999

This is not a type system flaw. TypeScript assumes developers will not use type assertions to subvert safety guarantees. The readonly types are a contract that the compiler enforces, but they are not a security boundary.

Compile-time vs runtime immutability layers

If runtime immutability is required, three strategies apply. First, return defensive copies. Clone the map before returning it, so mutations affect only the copy. Second, use an immutable data structure library like Immutable.js or Immer, which provides collections that cannot be mutated even at runtime. Third, use Object.freeze() on plain objects to prevent property changes, though this does not work on maps or sets.

Defensive copying has a performance cost. Cloning a large map on every read scales poorly. Immutable libraries add a dependency and require learning a new API. Object.freeze() is shallow and does not prevent nested mutations.

The pragmatic approach is to treat TypeScript's readonly types as the primary defense and add runtime protection only where necessary. A public API that crosses a trust boundary should return defensive copies. Internal code within a controlled codebase can rely on readonly types and code review to prevent misuse.

The key distinction is that readonly types catch accidental mutation by well-intentioned developers. Runtime immutability defends against adversarial code or JavaScript interop where the type system cannot help.

Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

The most common mistake is forgetting that ReadonlyMap is a shallow constraint. Developers assume that returning ReadonlyMap<string, Config> prevents all mutation, but if Config is a mutable object, its properties can still change.

interface Config {
  apiKey: string;
  timeout: number;
}

const configs = new Map<string, Config>([
  ["prod", { apiKey: "secret", timeout: 5000 }],
]);

function getConfigs(): ReadonlyMap<string, Config> {
  return configs;
}

const snapshot = getConfigs();
// snapshot.set("dev", { apiKey: "test", timeout: 1000 }); // Error
const prodConfig = snapshot.get("prod");
if (prodConfig) {
  prodConfig.timeout = 10000; // No error, modifies original
}

The fix is to make the value type readonly as well: ReadonlyMap<string, Readonly<Config>>. This prevents mutation of both the map and the objects it contains.

Shallow vs deep readonly protection

The second pitfall is returning a readonly view from a function but storing the result in a mutable variable. The type system allows assigning a ReadonlyMap to a Map variable if the declaration uses let without an explicit type annotation.

function getCache(): ReadonlyMap<string, number> {
  return new Map([["key", 1]]);
}

let cache = getCache(); // Type inferred as ReadonlyMap
cache.set("new", 2); // Compiler error

let mutableCache: Map<string, number> = getCache() as Map<string, number>;
mutableCache.set("new", 2); // Works but bypasses readonly intent

The solution is to always annotate variables that hold readonly collections with the readonly type. Do not rely on type inference to preserve the constraint.

Type annotation preserving readonly constraints in variable declarations

The third pitfall is using readonly types inconsistently across a codebase. One module returns Map, another returns ReadonlyMap, and developers cannot tell which functions might mutate shared state. The fix is to establish a convention: all functions that expose collections return readonly types unless mutation is explicitly part of the API contract.

This consistency matters. When readonly types are the default, a function signature that returns Map signals intent: this collection is meant to be mutated. The type system becomes documentation that the compiler enforces.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does ReadonlyMap have any runtime overhead compared to Map?

ReadonlyMap is a type annotation only. At runtime, a ReadonlyMap is a Map instance with no wrapper, proxy, or performance cost. The readonly constraint exists only at compile time.

Can I convert a Map to a ReadonlyMap without copying it?

Yes. A Map can be directly returned or assigned where a ReadonlyMap is expected because it satisfies the readonly interface structurally. No copying or conversion is needed.

How do I handle nested mutable objects inside a ReadonlyMap?

Use Readonly<T> recursively on the value type: ReadonlyMap<string, Readonly<Config>>. For deeply nested structures, consider a library like ts-essentials that provides DeepReadonly.

Why would I use ReadonlySet instead of a readonly array?

ReadonlySet provides O(1) membership checks with .has(), while arrays require O(n) iteration with .includes(). Use sets for large collections where membership testing is frequent.

Can I use ReadonlyMap with the new TypeScript 5.x features?

Yes. ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet work seamlessly with features like as const, satisfies, and the branded types pattern covered in TypeScript branded types.

Immutable Collections as Part of a Broader Type Safety Strategy

ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet are tools, not solutions. They prevent accidental mutation at compile time but do not eliminate all risks. A codebase that adopts these types must also establish conventions for when mutation is acceptable, how to handle runtime immutability requirements, and how to integrate with third-party code that expects mutable collections.

The broader pattern is to default to immutability and opt into mutation explicitly. Function parameters should use readonly types unless the function must modify the collection. Return types should expose readonly views unless the caller is expected to mutate the result. This approach scales because it makes mutation visible in the type signature.

The same principle applies to other TypeScript features. Use as const for configuration objects. Use Readonly<T> for interfaces that represent immutable state. Use branded types to prevent accidental mixing of semantically different values. Each feature reinforces the others, and the type system becomes a defense-in-depth strategy against entire classes of bugs.

Related patterns include typed routes in Next.js for compile-time URL safety and as const with satisfies for narrow literal types. These techniques combine to create codebases where invalid states are unrepresentable at the type level.

That covers the essential patterns for using ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet in production TypeScript. Apply these in your cache APIs, configuration systems, and shared state management, and the difference will be immediate. The bugs that never reach production because the compiler caught them are the ones that matter most.

articles.body_html:
What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

**Uncertain rewards. **Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

**Self-regulation. **In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

articles.body_html:
RepoDNA v1.4.0: An Original Logo, Branded Startup, and Reliability Improvements

RepoDNA v1.4.0 is now available.

This release represents a new step in the development of RepoDNA, my open-source, local-first repository intelligence and codebase archaeology project.

Rather than introducing another major analysis subsystem, v1.4.0 focuses on strengthening the application's identity, improving startup behavior, addressing accessibility details, and resolving several usability issues.

The central philosophy remains unchanged:

Understand your codebase. See its DNA.

What is RepoDNA?

RepoDNA helps developers understand software repositories beyond individual source files.

It analyzes information such as:

  • Repository structure and architecture
  • Programming languages and dependencies
  • Git history and repository evolution
  • Code quality and complexity signals
  • Project hotspots and findings
  • Evidence-backed reports and Project DNA cards

It also supports optional AI-assisted explanations grounded in repository analysis.

The goal is to turn complex repositories into information developers can explore, understand, and act on.

1. An original, hand-authored SVG logo

The most visible change in v1.4.0 is RepoDNA's new logo.

The design combines DNA-inspired geometry with code-graph relationships.

It uses a navy, blue, and teal color palette and was created directly from SVG vector geometry rather than AI-generated artwork.

Because the design is vector-based, it can be rendered consistently at different sizes.

The identity is now reflected across the web application, desktop application, PWA icons, and project branding.

A matching vector wordmark was also introduced.

2. A branded startup experience

The new release introduces branded startup screens for the web and desktop applications.

The startup experience is designed to display branding while the application initializes.

Importantly, the implementation does not intentionally delay application startup merely to keep the branding visible.

The objective is to provide a consistent first impression without sacrificing usability.

3. Accessibility improvements

One of the less visible but important fixes involves keyboard focus.

Following application initialization, keyboard focus could fail to move to the main content region after the startup screen had been displayed.

v1.4.0 addresses this transition.

Accessibility improvements like this matter because visual changes should not make the application harder to navigate using a keyboard.

4. More reliable deep links

The web deep-link parser also received a correction.

Previously, additional question marks within URL query values were not preserved correctly in every case.

The updated parser handles these values more reliably.

This is a relatively small change, but correct URL parsing is essential for predictable web application behavior.

5. Documentation and GitHub Action corrections

The documentation was also updated.

In particular, the FAQ previously contained an incorrect statement suggesting that no official GitHub Action existed.

The FAQ now points developers toward the maintained RepoDNA GitHub Action and its documentation.

This makes the integration options clearer for users.

6. Expanded ways to support the project

RepoDNA is an open-source project, and the release introduces PayPal.Me as an additional support option.

The new support link appears alongside existing options in the project documentation and interface.

Support remains entirely optional.

7. Testing and release validation

The release includes regression checks for startup branding and support links.

The release workflow also covers the Rust codebase, WebAssembly components, TypeScript, desktop application, documentation, and dependency advisories.

These checks help maintain consistency across the project's different distribution formats.

What has not changed?

RepoDNA remains focused on local-first development.

The core analysis features continue to function without requiring developers to upload their repositories to a cloud analysis service.

Optional AI capabilities remain separate from the main repository analysis process.

The purpose of RepoDNA is still to help developers understand the structure, evolution, and relationships within their software projects.

Try RepoDNA v1.4.0

The release provides distribution options for Windows, macOS, and Linux, together with command-line, WebAssembly, npm, and container workflows.

You can also explore the web version directly in your browser.

GitHub Release:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.4.0

Web Application:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

Source Code:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA

What's next?

The new visual identity creates a more consistent foundation for future releases.

Future development can continue expanding repository analysis capabilities, improving performance and usability, and refining the experience across platforms.

Feedback is especially valuable from developers working with complex repositories or experimenting with local-first development tools.

If RepoDNA sounds useful, consider exploring the source code, opening an issue, contributing, or sharing your experience.

RepoDNA — Understand your codebase. See its DNA.

articles.body_html:
EyeZen v1.2.0: Bringing Local-First Workspace Customization to the Browser

EyeZen v1.2.0 is officially available!

After building the desktop foundation of EyeZen with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript, I've reached a new milestone: a functional browser edition with local settings persistence and a dedicated documentation website.

Why a web edition?

EyeZen started as a desktop application focused on workspace personalization, comfort preferences, profiles and break routines.

However, many features—such as changing themes, creating profiles and organizing break reminders—don't require access to native operating-system APIs.

Version 1.2.0 makes these capabilities accessible directly from a browser.

What's new in v1.2.0?

1. EyeZen Web

The browser edition includes ten appearance themes, nine starter workspace profiles, customizable profiles, scheduled routines, break reminders and accessibility preferences.

Users can personalize their environment without installing the desktop application.

2. Persistent local browser settings

A major part of this release involved implementing reliable browser persistence.

EyeZen stores settings locally, validates saved data and handles malformed records rather than silently overwriting them.

Settings can also be exported and imported as JSON.

The web and desktop editions use compatible settings schemas, although synchronization is manual rather than automatic.

3. Permission-aware reminders

EyeZen supports optional in-app break reminders and notification functionality.

Browser notification permission is requested through an explicit user interaction.

Reminders depend on the active application or browser tab and remain subject to browser and operating-system restrictions.

4. A new documentation website

Version 1.2.0 also introduces comprehensive public documentation.

It covers:

  • Application features and configuration
  • Web versus desktop compatibility
  • Installation and setup
  • Privacy and local storage
  • Architecture and accessibility
  • Troubleshooting and frequently asked questions

5. Maintaining honest platform boundaries

The browser edition cannot tint unrelated desktop windows, enumerate physical monitors or change hardware brightness.

The installed desktop application retains optional software-based visual tint overlays on supported environments.

Neither edition claims medical benefits or hardware-level display calibration.

Communicating these differences clearly is important when building trustworthy cross-platform software.

Built with open technologies

The project uses:

  • Rust and Tauri 2 for native desktop functionality
  • React and TypeScript for the interface
  • Vite for web builds
  • GitHub Actions for automated builds and deployment
  • GitHub Pages for the static browser application and documentation

EyeZen is open source under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

Try EyeZen

Web edition: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/

Documentation: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/docs/

GitHub release: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen/releases/tag/v1.2.0

Source code: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen

What's next?

EyeZen will continue evolving through better workspace customization, platform compatibility, accessibility improvements and stronger real-device testing.

If you use EyeZen or work with Rust, Tauri, TypeScript or cross-platform applications, I'd welcome your feedback and contributions.

What would you prioritize next for EyeZen?
