articles.body_html:
How to Keep Client-Side Animation From Taking Over Your Next.js Architecture

A single animated section can quietly change the architecture of an otherwise server-first Next.js page.

The hero needs pointer tracking, so "use client" appears at the top of the file.

Then a feature section needs a scroll timeline.

Later, someone adds a WebGL background that depends on browser APIs.

Before long, a page that originally needed a few interactive pieces has most of its component tree living behind a client boundary.

The animation still works.

The architecture has drifted.

In the App Router, "use client" defines a client module boundary. Once you cross it, modules imported into that client graph are part of the browser-side application.

So the useful rule is not:

Avoid client-side animation.

It is:

Put the client boundary around the smallest piece of interaction that actually needs the browser.

Everything else can stay server-first.

The problem is boundary creep

Most animation requirements are legitimate reasons to run code in the browser.

You might need:

  • window
  • pointer position
  • layout measurement
  • scroll progress
  • ResizeObserver
  • IntersectionObserver
  • an animation timeline
  • Canvas
  • WebGL
  • component state

None of those automatically mean the entire section or page should become a Client Component.

Imagine a product hero containing:

  • a heading
  • supporting copy
  • a CTA
  • pricing or product data
  • one animated visual

Only one part needs browser-side behavior.

If the whole hero gets "use client", the rendering boundary now reflects the needs of the animation rather than the needs of the interface.

That tends to spread.

Future developers see a client-owned section and add more client-only state to it. Server-renderable content becomes coupled to browser code. Animation dependencies start creeping upward through the component tree.

The better question is:

Which component actually owns the interaction?

That component should usually own the client boundary too.

Keep "use client" as low as practical

Consider this:

"use client"

export default function Hero() {
  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Build faster</h1>
      <p>Server-renderable marketing content.</p>
      <AnimatedProduct />
    </section>
  )
}

It works.

But the entire Hero is now part of the client module graph because one child needs animation.

A cleaner split is:

export default function Hero() {
  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Build faster</h1>
      <p>Server-renderable marketing content.</p>
      <AnimatedProduct />
    </section>
  )
}

Then isolate the animated piece:

"use client"

export function AnimatedProduct() {
  return <div>{/* animation logic */}</div>
}

Now the browser-specific behavior lives where it belongs.

The surrounding content can remain authored and rendered as Server Components while only the animated leaf enters the client graph.

This becomes much more useful when the animation also owns:

  • event listeners
  • observers
  • GSAP timelines
  • scroll triggers
  • pointer state
  • resize handling
  • cleanup

A good animation boundary tends to keep those responsibilities together.

Server-rendered content can still pass through a client wrapper

There is another pattern that is easy to miss.

Sometimes the animation needs to wrap content, but it does not need to own that content.

For example:

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <Reveal>
      <article>
        <h2>Server-rendered content</h2>
        <p>This content does not need client-side state.</p>
      </article>
    </Reveal>
  )
}

Then:

"use client"

export function Reveal({
  children,
}: {
  children: React.ReactNode
}) {
  return <div>{children}</div>
}

The important detail is the direction of composition.

The Server Component composes the content and passes it into the Client Component as children. The client module is not reaching back and importing a Server Component directly.

That pattern is useful for:

  • reveal wrappers
  • viewport-triggered sections
  • animated shells
  • carousels containing server-provided markup
  • interactive containers
  • transition wrappers

It lets the interaction stay client-side without moving all meaningful content there too.

Values crossing the boundary still need to follow React and Next.js serialization rules where applicable. Client-only functions and browser state should remain on the client side.

Before adding an animation library, ask whether CSS is enough

A surprising amount of motion does not need client-side JavaScript at all.

For example:

.card {
  transform: translateY(0);
  opacity: 1;
  transition:
    transform 220ms ease,
    opacity 220ms ease;
}

.card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px);
}

No hooks.

No animation runtime.

No lifecycle.

No "use client".

This is not an argument for replacing Motion or GSAP with CSS everywhere.

A hover state and a pinned scroll sequence are different problems.

The useful rule is to choose the smallest mechanism that solves the interaction.

CSS is often enough for:

  • hover feedback
  • color transitions
  • simple opacity
  • transforms
  • underlines
  • basic enter/exit effects where state is already available in CSS

A text reveal should not need a 3D pipeline.

Motion does not require client ownership of the whole section

Motion works naturally with React, so it is easy to let the client boundary expand around it.

That still is not necessary.

If one card needs gesture state or animation hooks, that card can own the client-side behavior.

The section containing twelve cards does not automatically need to become client-owned.

There is also an important current Next.js nuance here.

Motion provides motion/react-client for rendering Motion components from React Server Component contexts.

That does not mean all Motion behavior suddenly runs on the server.

Hooks, gesture logic, browser-dependent measurements, stateful interaction, and other client-only behavior still belong behind an appropriate Client Component boundary.

So think about what the component actually needs.

A simple animated element and a drag interaction have very different client requirements even if both use Motion.

Imperative animation needs a clear owner

Things become more architectural once you introduce imperative systems such as:

  • GSAP timelines
  • ScrollTrigger
  • custom observers
  • layout measurement
  • manual event listeners
  • resize logic

These all create lifecycle responsibilities.

The component that owns the affected DOM should usually own those responsibilities too.

Avoid one large page-level animation controller that reaches into unrelated sections.

Something like this is easier to reason about:

FeatureStory
├── owns its DOM
├── creates its timeline
├── creates its ScrollTriggers
├── handles its resize logic
└── cleans everything up on unmount

If another section has its own animation system, let that section own it separately.

Why?

Because page-level animation scripts tend to become brittle once the layout changes.

A section becomes conditional.

Another moves into a nested layout.

A mobile breakpoint changes the DOM.

One route preserves part of the tree while another unmounts it.

Suddenly the question "who cleans this animation up?" has no obvious answer.

Local ownership keeps animation architecture composable.

Do not make the animation timeline your page structure

Scroll animation is where this mistake shows up frequently.

Suppose a desktop section pins a product image while five text states appear as the user scrolls.

On mobile, you might not want the pinned experience at all.

The content should still work as:

Feature 1
Visual 1

Feature 2
Visual 2

Feature 3
Visual 3

The animation is a presentation layer over meaningful content.

It should not be the only thing holding that content together.

That gives you a much healthier fallback when:

  • the viewport changes
  • reduced motion is enabled
  • JS fails
  • the animation library changes
  • the creative direction gets simplified later

WebGL and Canvas deserve their own island

WebGL is an even stronger case for isolation.

A 3D hero might depend on:

  • Canvas
  • WebGL
  • Three.js
  • React Three Fiber
  • shaders
  • textures
  • pointer input
  • requestAnimationFrame
  • viewport dimensions
  • device pixel ratio

None of those requirements mean the heading or CTA should become client-owned.

A better architecture looks like this:

Server-rendered Hero
├── Heading
├── Copy
├── CTA
└── Client WebGL Island

The meaningful content remains ordinary HTML.

The renderer stays isolated.

This also makes it easier to:

  • provide a static fallback
  • simplify the effect on mobile
  • load the renderer later
  • reduce GPU work
  • remove the scene without rewriting the content structure

If the WebGL scene is expensive or below the fold, it may also be a good candidate for lazy loading.

ssr: false is useful, but it is not an architecture

When a package depends directly on browser APIs, the quickest reaction is often:

dynamic(() => import("./Scene"), {
  ssr: false,
})

Sometimes that is exactly right.

But in the App Router, there is an important constraint:

ssr: false must be configured from a Client Component.

So for a browser-only renderer, the structure might look like:

// SceneClient.tsx
"use client"

import dynamic from "next/dynamic"

const Scene = dynamic(() => import("./Scene"), {
  ssr: false,
})

export function SceneClient() {
  return <Scene />
}

Your Server Component can then render SceneClient.

This is a useful browser-only boundary.

It still does not answer the rest of the architecture.

ssr: false tells Next.js not to server-render that component.

It does not decide:

  • how large the client island should be
  • whether the renderer should load immediately
  • where meaningful content belongs
  • who owns cleanup
  • whether mobile gets a fallback
  • whether reduced motion changes the effect
  • whether the animation should pause offscreen

Those are separate decisions.

A whole page made client-only because one component touches window is very different from a small isolated renderer that genuinely has no server representation.

Lazy loading and disabling SSR solve different problems

These two decisions are often bundled together, but they answer different questions.

Lazy loading asks:

When should this code be downloaded?

Disabling SSR asks:

Should this component render on the server at all?

A heavy scene below the fold might benefit from lazy loading.

A tiny client interaction at the top of the page probably does not need elaborate deferral.

A browser-only WebGL renderer may reasonably use both dynamic loading and ssr: false.

A simple Motion element may need neither.

Keeping these decisions separate prevents dynamic() from becoming a generic wrapper around every animation component.

Keep global animation providers smaller than you think

Once a site starts accumulating motion, it is tempting to create one global animation layer.

Some shared configuration is useful.

For example:

  • reduced-motion policy
  • transition defaults
  • common easing values
  • feature flags
  • interaction preferences

But shared policy does not mean shared implementation.

You probably do not need one global controller owning:

  • every ScrollTrigger
  • every observer
  • every timeline
  • the cursor
  • all page animations
  • every animation state

Next.js generally benefits from placing providers as deep as practical.

The same approach works well for motion.

If only the marketing section needs an animation provider, put it there.

If only one route has a custom cursor, do not make the root layout own it.

Keep global policy global. Keep local animation local.

Pause work the user cannot see

The client boundary is only the first part of the problem.

Once the animation has hydrated, you still need to decide when it should run.

A Canvas scene rendering in a hidden tab is still consuming resources.

An offscreen particle effect may still be animating.

A cursor trail may remain subscribed to pointer movement even after the relevant component is gone if cleanup is incomplete.

Depending on the effect, consider:

  • pausing render loops when the page is hidden
  • suspending expensive work while offscreen
  • disconnecting observers
  • removing event listeners
  • killing timelines on unmount
  • reducing visual complexity on mobile
  • lowering WebGL rendering cost
  • providing a static fallback

One animation doing unnecessary work may not be noticeable.

Five or six independently animated sections can make those assumptions add up quickly.

A practical architecture checklist

Before adding another animation to an App Router project, ask:

Question Preferred direction
Can CSS solve it? Keep it out of the client runtime
Does it need hooks, state, or browser APIs? Use a small Client Component
Does it need an imperative timeline? Give that timeline a local owner
Does it create listeners or observers? Keep setup and cleanup together
Does it contain meaningful content? Keep that content in HTML where possible
Does it require Canvas or WebGL? Isolate the renderer
Is the renderer expensive or below the fold? Consider lazy loading
Can it only exist in the browser? Use an appropriate client-only boundary
Does it need shared motion policy? Place the provider as deep as practical
Can it stop while hidden? Pause it
What happens with reduced motion? Simplify the interaction intentionally
What happens on touch devices? Design a real fallback

This is the kind of checklist that stops animation from gradually becoming application architecture.

How source-first effects help with this

This is also where source-first interaction libraries can be useful.

For example, Hyperiux Vault provides React and Next.js interaction patterns as editable source.

The useful part from an architecture perspective is not simply that the effect exists.

It is that you can inspect:

  • where the client boundary begins
  • what dependencies the effect uses
  • how lifecycle and cleanup are handled
  • what should change for mobile or browser-only rendering

That makes it easier to fit an effect into your existing architecture instead of restructuring the application around an opaque package.

Vault's installation docs also distinguish effects that rely on things such as scroll state, pointer movement, layout measurement, timelines, Canvas, or WebGL from components that do not inherently require the same client-side footprint.

Vault does not solve Next.js architecture for you.

Next.js still defines the rendering model. Motion, GSAP, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and browser APIs still bring their own constraints.

Editable source simply makes those constraints easier to inspect and adapt.

The goal is not zero client JavaScript

A creative Next.js site is allowed to use the browser.

Some interactions genuinely require it.

Scroll-linked storytelling needs scroll state.

Dragging needs pointer input.

A page transition needs navigation state.

A custom cursor needs pointer events.

WebGL needs a renderer.

Trying to eliminate client JavaScript entirely would eliminate useful interaction along with it.

The goal is architectural proportion.

One hero measuring the viewport does not mean the page should become client-owned.

One Canvas component does not mean the route should disable SSR.

One animated wrapper does not mean its content needs to move into a client module.

Let the animation own the browser code it actually needs.

Then stop the boundary there.

If you want to inspect how more complex React and Next.js interaction patterns handle those boundaries in editable source, you can browse the Hyperiux Vault effects library.

A good interaction can be ambitious. Its client boundary does not have to be.

articles.title: The Software Entropy in the AI Era
articles.description: TL;DR: I ran an experiment with AI-augmented development. In one month we produced 400k+ lines of...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: I ran an experiment with AI-augmented development. In one month we produced 400k+ lines of code, 150 features, 240 fixes and 50 refactors, then the entropy accelerated and the velocity collapsed. What normally takes years of accumulated technical debt across multiple teams happened in weeks.

Hi there, my name is Takah, I'm a Principal Software Engineer from Brazil. In the past months I've been conducting a few experiments on how to adapt our SDLC and explore new ways of working with AI, both enabling non-engineers to code in our repos and also enhancing every guard-rail, guideline and common market standards to support this type of workflow.

What Is Software Entropy?

But let's circle back to the title of this article: what is Software Entropy? First of all, what is entropy? I'll freely give one interpretation that entropy, borrowed from thermodynamics, is the natural tendency toward disorder or uncertainty in a system, and what is exactly software entropy? I'd say its the natural tendency of any given software and system to disorder, when new features are being added, new modules, new fixes, quick-wins, a hacky solution to fix or deliver something in time, or to prevent another incident, regardless of the most architectural pre-definition and future-proof hexagonal multi-flexible, composable and any other blazingly fast buzzword you wanna add, it's impossible to predict and prevent all use-cases beforehand, that's why entropy always end up happening.

Software entropy is not a bug, it's a fundamental property of any system that grows. The question is never if it will happen, its how fast, and whether you have the mechanisms to manage it.

What Does AI Have to Do With Software Entropy?

And what AI has to do with Software Entropy? Like i said one of the experiments i did was me a Software engineer and 2 other designers, which we had the challenge of developing a whole new experience of a chat and we wanted to leverage the AI ecosystem at its maximum.

So first, before any line of code, i aligned the scope, contracts, and overall architecture of the project:

  • Tech stack
  • Repository setup, code structure, architectural guidelines
  • AI guidelines: agents, skills, context files for testing, styling, developing new features, feature-branches

And after the initial setup we had, and helping them setup their own setup with claude, our internal ai-proxy, repository, vpns, etc we started developing. And at the beginning it was awesome. The guidelines and setup were satisfactory, features seemed to be right, we were adding one feature after another with autonomy, tests, coverage, and apparently following the project guidelines.

But whats the problem?

The Turn: Week Three

After 3 weeks we had a codebase with more than 400k lines, dozens of features, animations, micro-interactions that would maybe take several sprints to be made if they were handcrafted by a team of engineers. But at this moment things started to break down:

  • Each feature velocity started to decline
  • New behaviours that interacted with previous states started to skyrocket race-conditions
  • One new feature broke 3 other working ones
  • A simple feature that previously took a few hours now took days

And we had to circle back and analyze what was happening.

The guidelines and guard-rails that were previously added were not enough, because even with a strict guideline saying to our models and setup: "Use X technology or Y Architecture or Z state management tool in this way," the probabilist nature of LLMs still were delusional.

We had several features that reimplemented different state machines, did full animations, sound, charts from scratch while it was already solved in a sibling part of the application, and one of the signs were the codebase growth, it was exponentially growing in number of lines and files.

To give you a sense of the scale, in roughly one month we accumulated:

  • 150 features added
  • 240 fixes applied
  • 50 refactors performed, with refactors as large as removing more than 50k lines of code in a single one

And I'm not alone in this, the data from 2026 tells the same story across the industry. The 2025 DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development report found that a 25% increase in AI adoption is associated with a 7.2% decrease in delivery stability, because AI allows developers to generate code much faster and it often leads to larger batch sizes, which are slower to review and more prone to creating system instability. New Relic's 2026 State of AI Coding report, which surveyed 200 technology leaders, found that while 94% of them rate AI-generated code as higher quality at review time, 78% report more incidents once it ships and 82% experienced at least one production failure tied to AI-generated code in the past six months. They call this agent debt, the rapid accumulation of unvetted architectural logic that triggers production incidents down the line. And a systematic review of 34 studies covering 2,847 developers found that technical debt principal increased by 1.8 person-days per 1,000 AI-generated lines of code, with the debt ratio doubling within 6 months without mitigation.

The Fix: Tightening the Guard-Rails

To fix that we had to do several fixes, refactors, and with each fix and refactor to strictly tighten the guard-rails, tests, and add custom deterministic tools to truly ensure that the code was following each guideline. In practice this meant:

  • AI guard-rails in agents: direct instructions, specific skills and context files that enforced architectural patterns
  • Deterministic tools: lint rules, pipeline validations and custom checks that verified architectural conformance before merge
  • Strict refactoring cycles: regular mandatory refactoring capacity to reduce the debt principal
  • Expert oversight: a specialized developer actively enhancing the guidelines, understanding what to use, what not to use, how to fix, and correcting the AI to follow new strict rules

In the end result the AI usage was a success, within a month we developed something that would take months to be made handcrafted, but at what cost?

If a specialized developer was not present enhancing the guidelines, understanding what to use, what not to use, how to fix, and actively enhancing its guard-rails this codebase was doomed to failure. Or maybe a full refactor or depriorization due to the effort of maintaining it.

The Exponential Decline of the Codebase

So whats my conclusion? All that happening within a month its the same thing i saw happening during years of a codebase, it normally takes months of multiple developers, teams, and technical debts accumulated to reach the same level of entropy and disorder where each new feature was breaking 3 others. What I'm calling the exponential decline of the codebase is not just a metaphor, its what happens when the rate of entropy generation outpaces the rate of human oversight by an order of magnitude.

The IEEE Computer Society puts it bluntly: "Standing between such problematic AI output and other downstream disasters? Software engineers. The value of engineers with the software lifecycle knowledge needed to guide and oversee AI assistants and their output is immeasurable."

The arXiv paper "Beyond the 'Diff'" defines agentic entropy as "a systemic drift that traditional code diff-based and HCXAI methods fail to capture, as they address local outputs rather than global agentic behaviour," and notes that "functional checks (e.g., confirming that the code runs) can thus mask deeper architectural violations and security gaps, producing an illusion of rapid progress while drift accumulates beneath the surface."

The AI era is awesome, but without proper follow-up and deep specialized people understanding whats being written and which software engineering strategies, architecture and design patterns to follow, it will exponentially increase the software entropy. Gartner predicts that by 2029, 60% of organizations will adopt smaller software engineering teams at scale, up from 15% in 2026. But smaller teams with AI does not mean no engineers, it means engineers with different skills, architects, overseers, guard-rail builders. The ACM Technology Policy Council's TechBrief on vibe coding warns that it "often skips over core engineering practices that ensure systems are secure, reliable, and maintainable," and their lead author Simson Garfinkel says it directly: "It's making developers dramatically more effective, but it's also introducing security vulnerabilities, increasing technical debt, and producing code that can be difficult to maintain."

A Reflection for Engineering Leaders

If you're a manager, head of engineering, VP or CTO reading this, i want you to reflect on a few things:

  • How are you aspiring your org to be? Are you designing for a future where AI does the coding and engineers do the oversight, or one where engineers use AI as a tool while retaining architectural ownership?
  • Where are your gaps? Do you have mechanisms to detect software entropy as it accumulates, deterministic guard-rails and not just guidelines, engineers who can recognize when the AI is drifting from architectural intent?
  • Whats your oversight model? The data from New Relic shows that 62% of technology leaders report their teams trust AI-generated code enough to ship it to production without line-by-line manual verification, is that a risk you're willing to take?

My Disclosure on AI

In that way, i don't dislike Agentic Coding, neither the idea of non-engineers coding, my conclusion is that the current state of ai tools are not ready yet to be driven by full Ai enthusiasts, software engineers are going to exist, this is the new normal we should not fear Ai we should embrace these new tools and understand how we could be more productive and have more time to focus in new strategies, features, design patterns, career, our mental and physical health and our familly not only delivering more value to our shareholders.

The illusion that a single person with AI can replace a team of engineers is just that, an illusion. What we experienced in one month is what happens when you remove the expertise from the loop. The entropy accelerates, the velocity collapses, and the cost compounds. Software engineers are still necessary, the question is, are we building organizations that know how to use them?

articles.title: How do you manage CORS for thousands of customer domains? Per tenant, with three answers instead of two
articles.description: Our domain registry can stop answering. It can also answer that a customer's domain is no longer...
articles.body_html:
Our domain registry can stop answering. It can also answer that a customer's domain is no longer allowed. Both cases leave the proxy without a usable current list, but only the first gives us a reason to reuse an older one.

That distinction shaped our per-tenant CORS cache. We keep valid results for 15 minutes and a fallback copy for 24 hours. An authoritative refusal erases that fallback, so the next outage cannot bring a removed domain back.

One domain per customer

At GoodBarber, the web version of each customer app has its own domain, either a platform subdomain or a custom one. We are piloting a proxy that lets widgets call third-party APIs while their private keys stay on the server. Its CORS policy has to fit that domain model, even while the service itself is limited to a small pilot.

Our first static allowlist was manageable for five pilot apps. It could not follow the platform's thousands of domains as customers changed them. Allowing arbitrary origins would also defeat the restriction we wanted; PortSwigger documents that mistake in its guide to CORS misconfigurations. We needed to resolve the list for each tenant.

The preflight does not know who is calling

An actual API call carries a short-lived token naming the tenant. Its preflight arrives earlier, without that token: CORS preflight requests do not carry credentials. We receive an origin, a proposed method and a list of header names, so the token cannot supply the tenant for this lookup.

The request path can. It contains an opaque connector handle belonging to one tenant. We resolve the handle, then the tenant's domains. Because this happens before token validation, the lookup must also tolerate requests from arbitrary callers.

Origins, exactly as a browser sends them

The registry returns a domain. A browser sends an origin, and the comparison is string equality, so the list has to be built the way a browser would write it.

  • The default port for the scheme is omitted: :443 for HTTPS, :80 for HTTP. Non-default ports are kept.
  • A custom domain yields two origins, with and without www, since customers publish both. A subdomain of ours yields exactly one.
  • An internationalised domain is converted to punycode, which is what the browser sends.
  • The response carries the one matching origin and Vary: Origin, as MDN recommends for an explicit origin. Never *, and Origin: null never matches.

A miss needs a reason

Once the main cache entry expires, the registry lookup can produce three different outcomes:

The registry… What the proxy serves What it stores
answers with domains those origins the list for 15 minutes, and a second copy for 24 hours
cannot be reached, answers an error or sends garbage the 24-hour copy, if there is one the main entry again, for 60 seconds
answers clearly that the tenant has no usable domain no CORS headers an empty list for 60 seconds, and it deletes the 24-hour copy

The outage path borrows the idea of stale-if-error. Apps can keep using a previously accepted origin while the registry is unavailable. Caching that fallback decision for 60 seconds reduces repeated lookups; it does not by itself guarantee a global request-rate bound when concurrent misses occur.

An explicit removal has a different meaning. If we kept its old list, a later registry outage could restore the revoked origin from the 24-hour copy. Deleting that copy makes the refusal survive the outage too.

The pre-auth path is bounded

Before any I/O, we check the handle's shape and hash it for use in cache keys. Unknown handles are cached as unknown for 60 seconds. If the shared cache is unavailable, an in-process cache lasting 5 seconds, with at most 4,096 entries, limits repeated database work.

The preflight path responds with 204. If neither the lookup nor its permitted fallback yields an allowed origin, the response omits CORS headers. Dependency errors therefore do not become a 500, and the browser cannot proceed with the cross-origin call after an unsuccessful preflight.

Treat your cache as input

The cache is shared infrastructure, so what comes out of it is validated like anything else that crosses a boundary. Values are JSON, never pickled objects. Every list read back is checked, item by item, against the same pattern that judged it on the way in. A value that exists but fails that check is ignored and logged as a tampering signal.

Review found a mismatch here. Normalisation accepted a hostname containing an underscore, but cache validation used a stricter rule and rejected it. That value would have been repeatedly written, discarded and fetched again, leaving both caches ineffective for the tenant. Applying the same rule on write and read removed the disagreement.

CORS is not the lock

These responses govern browser access. A client such as curl does not enforce them, so actual requests still undergo token validation and the connector's permission checks. Using an older CORS list leaves those checks in place; it changes which browser origins may read the responses.

The feature and its hardening landed on July 23, six minutes apart: the second commit is the adversarial review of the first. The module has 48 tests: normalisation, the three outcomes, the bounds of the pre-auth path, and the few static origins we add on top.

To test the distinction, cache an allowed domain, have the registry explicitly remove it, then make the registry unavailable. The domain should remain absent. Testing an outage alone would miss the case where a cache reverses a decision it had already received.

CampusCore v1.0.0: Building an Open-Source Student Management System

Managing academic information involves more than storing student records. Institutions also need attendance tracking, academic structures, marks, grading, reporting, staff workflows, and administrative tools.

I started building CampusCore to bring these essential operations into a single, maintainable, self-hosted application.

Today, CampusCore reaches its first stable release: v1.0.0.

What is CampusCore?

CampusCore is an MIT-licensed, open-source student and academic management system.

It's built around a modular backend architecture and a responsive web client.

The objective is to make academic administration easier to organize while keeping the codebase understandable and extensible.

Features in v1.0.0

Student and academic management

CampusCore includes student profiles, guardian information, academic years, classes, sections, enrollment, and subject management.

Attendance and assessments

The system supports attendance, leave workflows, marks, grading rules, report-card data, and timetables.

Administrative tools

Additional capabilities include staff records, announcements, dashboard metrics, global search, bulk-import validation, exports, institution settings, and audit history.

Web experience

The React/TypeScript frontend provides responsive layouts, theme preferences, accessible navigation, printable report styling, and a Progressive Web App shell.

Technology stack

The project uses:

  • ASP.NET Core 9 for the backend API
  • Entity Framework Core and PostgreSQL for persistence
  • React 19 and TypeScript for the frontend
  • Vite for web development and builds
  • Docker for containerized deployment
  • GitHub Actions for automated validation and release workflows

The backend follows a modular monolith approach, separating domain logic, application services, infrastructure, and API responsibilities.

What ships with v1.0.0?

The release includes self-hosted API server packages for Windows x64, Linux x64, and Apple Silicon macOS, along with the Web/PWA bundle.

There is also a browser companion package for developer installation and an Android debug APK for testing.

The API executables are not standalone desktop applications. They require PostgreSQL and appropriate server configuration. The Android APK is not a production or Google Play release.

Engineering and reliability

CampusCore includes automated tests, deployment checks, production configuration validation, database migration support, and backup/recovery tooling.

These foundations are important because academic applications need more than a functional user interface. They must also account for authorization, data integrity, operational failures, and deployment safety.

What's next?

This first stable release establishes the foundation for continued development.

Future work will focus on stronger deployment workflows, platform packaging, additional testing, and improvements based on practical feedback.

Try CampusCore

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/campuscore

Version 1.0.0 Release:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/campuscore/releases/tag/v1.0.0

Developer Website:

https://sanskarin.github.io

If you are interested in educational technology, ASP.NET Core, React, or open-source development, I'd welcome your feedback.

Issues, suggestions, and contributions are appreciated.

CampusCore v1.0.0 — One platform for essential academic operations.

articles.title: How many tools should an MCP server have? I measured 5 to 100 in Claude Code, Codex and Gemini
articles.description: Most advice about MCP server design says keep the tool count small. I read 91 sources: 38 say design...
articles.body_html:
Most advice about MCP server design says keep the tool count small. I read 91 sources: 38 say design fewer tools, 20 give a number (mostly 10–20), and only 10 measured tool count against accuracy at all. Then I measured it: 1,932 runs, three clients, 5 to 100 tools. On today's top models accuracy didn't move, not with 100 tools, not with look-alikes, not even with vague names. What moves is cost, and how much depends on how your client loads tools, not on the model. Since 2026 all three clients hide most of your tool list from the model by default, which makes tool names matter in a new way.

MCP server best practices nobody measured

Before measuring anything, I read 91 sources on MCP server design, every one of them in full: 21 official docs, 28 vendor blogs, 20 independent blogs, 2 forum threads and 20 papers. 38 of them say to curate fewer tools, 22 say to keep the visible set small through search or deferred loading, and 8 recommend code mode, where one or two tools run code. None say to expose everything.

20 sources give a number: 5–8 (Workato), 5–15 (Phil Schmid), under 10 per namespace and under 20 (OpenAI), 10–20 (Gemini, Speakeasy), 30–50 (Claude docs), "40 is the knee" (Archestra). Only 3 of those 20 numbers come from the source's own measurement. Two of the most repeated claims don't hold up. "Models break at 30 tools" traces back to the RAG-MCP paper, which counted MCP servers in the prompt, not tools. "Cursor won't take more than 40 tools" stopped being true when the cap was removed in January 2026.

Of the 91 sources, 46 are opinion and 8 cite someone else. 37 measured something, but only 10 measured tool count against accuracy: 7 papers, GitHub's Copilot (40 → 13 tools for +2–5 points), LangChain and one informal test on a 1.7B model. The rest measured tokens or compared MCP with a CLI, which isn't a tool-count measurement. Even on grouping the advice splits: 15 sources recommend workflow tools, 15 grouped tools, and 3 one tool per operation, and those 3 argue from permission prompts, not accuracy.

How I measured it

I built a fake server with 100 realistic file and document tools, with honest names and schemas. Some of them are deliberately confusable, like pdf_compress, pdf_optimize and image_compress. It also has a grouped variant, with 7 tools covering 50 operations, and a vague-names variant. None of the tools touches a file: the server's call log is the judge.

The agents got 18 tasks with known answers, 10 of them ambiguous, at N = 5, 10 … 50, 75 and 100 tools, two times each. The clients were Claude Code (Opus 5.5) with tool search on and off, Codex CLI (GPT-6.1-sol) and Antigravity (Gemini 3.1 Pro), each on its own subscription. All measurements are on GitHub: the report, results.csv and the raw log of every run.

How many MCP tools is too many?

Every run with separate tools was fully correct, from 5 to 100 tools, in all three clients and in both Claude Code modes. That includes every ambiguous task and the 50 extra look-alike tools at 75–100. So on Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1-sol and Gemini 3.1 Pro (October 2026), "fewer tools = more accurate" didn't show up in this range, which matches the survey's caveat that degradation depends heavily on the model.

Claude Code's tool search never hid the right tool. Every run made exactly one ToolSearch call, as its first action, and selected tools by exact name. The model sees all tool names up front and picks between look-alikes from the names alone, before it reads any schema.

What MCP tools really cost in Claude Code, Codex and Gemini

Input tokens, averaged over 36 runs per cell (18 tasks × 2). Every one of these runs was fully correct, so the table shows cost only.

Client How tools reach the model First call: 5 / 50 / 100 tools Per run: 5 / 50 / 100 tools One more tool (first call / per run)
Claude Code (Opus 5.5), tool search on (default) Names only; schemas loaded on demand with ToolSearch 3.9k / 4.6k / 5.4k 13.8k / 17.4k / 19.9k ~15 / 79 tokens
Claude Code (Opus 5.5), tool search off Every full schema in the prompt 4.1k / 11.7k / 20.2k 9.3k / 27.9k / 48.6k 169 / 429 tokens
Codex CLI (GPT-6.1-sol) Code mode: schemas never in the prompt; the model searches them with code 13.2k flat 45.3k / 61.4k / 78.2k 0 / 408 tokens
Antigravity (Gemini 3.1 Pro) Names only; schema file opened on demand 3.8k / 4.1k / 4.3k 15.7k / 20.5k / 18.6k ~5 tokens / flat

Tool search is the switch that matters in Claude Code. It's on by default: only tool names go into the prompt, and the model loads the schemas it needs with one ToolSearch call. That extra call makes it dearer than loading everything below about 19 tools, and cheaper above: 59% less input per run at 100 tools. It's off behind a proxy or on Azure Foundry, with older models, with ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false, or with --tools "". Fewer tokens didn't mean a cheaper run, though: at list price a run with search on cost $0.047 against $0.038 with it off at 100 tools, because cached input is cheap and the search adds a call. What search saves is context, not money.

The trap I fell into: my isolation flag switched off Claude Code's tool search, and I first reported the "search off" numbers as normal. A single flag changed the first-call cost by 4x.

Grouping MCP tools: cheaper in one client, worse in another

With every schema loaded (Claude Code, search off), 7 grouped tools cost what 14 separate ones do, at 100% accuracy. With tool search on, Claude Code's default, grouping barely matters: 16.1k input tokens per run against 17.4k for 50 separate tools. Grouping pays off only where every schema is loaded upfront.

Antigravity is the one place in the whole experiment where accuracy dropped, to 89%. Gemini skipped reading the schema of the multi-operation tool, guessed operation names such as delete, help and fake_op, and ran a wrong one 3 times.

Do names decide? Vague names under deferred loading

For this variant I kept the same 100 tools and the same descriptions, and gave the tools careless names: optimize_file, optimize_document, process_image, combine_files, handle_pages. Accuracy held: 276 of 276 runs were correct, and no wrong tool was executed. The descriptions decided the answer.

But wherever the model sees names first, the names decided the path to that answer. In Claude Code with search on, honest names let the model load exactly the schema it needed in 69 of 72 runs; with vague names, in 7 of 72. It fell back to keyword searches, the schemas loaded per run went from 1.6 to 7.6 at 100 tools (23 in one run), and input grew by 21%. Gemini opened the wrong tool's schema first in 34 of 72 runs, and in 10 runs it probed wrong tools with empty arguments. My server rejected those empty calls; on a real server, a tool with no required arguments would have run. Gemini's input grew by 38% at 100 tools.

Where every description is already in the prompt, vague names changed nothing: Claude Code with search off didn't notice them. Good descriptions rescue bad names only where the model can see them. Codex searches the definitions with code, so names barely mattered there either.

The names that misled most often: "3 JPGs into one PDF" led to combine_files, which actually merges PDFs; "shrink a PNG" led to optimize_image; and pptx and docx to PDF got mixed up between convert_file and convert_document.

MCP tool naming: dots, prefixes and the 64-character budget

Names that every client can call use letters, digits, _ and -, up to 64 characters. The Claude API rejects dots, and some clients rename dots on their side. Those 64 characters are also shared: Claude Code calls your tool mcp__<server>__<tool>, so a long server name eats into the budget. One more surprise from the runs: Gemini's API rejected tool schemas with integer enums in one eager-loading run.

So what should you do?

  • Don't cut tools for accuracy's sake on frontier models; cut or defer them for cost and context, and check which of your users' clients loads them eagerly.
  • Name tools by action and object, not by generic verbs: names are now the first thing a model reads, and vague ones cost extra reads and risk a wrong call.
  • Write descriptions a model can tell apart: that's what kept accuracy at 100% with look-alikes and vague names.
  • Don't group blindly: test in the clients your users run.
  • Measure your own server. This worklore story walks through the same benchmark step by step, and your agent can run it against your server.

Limitations

Fake tools and one domain (files). Three frontier models only: smaller and older models weren't tested, and that's where the measured sources in the survey report drops. Direct tasks with no long reasoning alongside, so context crowding wasn't measured. Vague names were tested with good descriptions only, not with both vague. Token counts include each client's overhead. Some sizes weren't run in every lane, and the Codex vague-names lane has 60 of 72 runs because of a usage limit. And it's one point in time: October 2026.

Did you choose your tool count and names by measurement or by advice? What did you measure?

articles.title: Requests, Promises, Assertions, and Declarations: Rewriting Our AI Agent Workflow as a 1986 'Committed Speech' Machine
articles.description: Why do 200-line agent prompts, Asimov's Three Laws, and sequential pre-landing checklists all fail the same way? How Fernando Flores's 1986 Committed Speech, Nuel Belnap's 1977 4-Valued Logic, and Tony Hoare's 1978 CSP turned our Makefile and init.d workflow into a self-healing Commitment Machine.
articles.body_html:
How Fernando Flores's 1986 Conversation for Action, Nuel Belnap's 1977 four-valued logic, and a 1976 HP 2000 BASIC resequencer replaced 130 lines of defensive prompt lawyering—and solved the exact state-machine bug that crashed both the Star Trek M-5 computer and my Piper Arrow.

"What did you do for AI? I brought the scars. What did you do for humanity? I asked my curiosity-based questions, and the world changed around me."

— Randal L. Schwartz

1. Portland, Thanksgiving 1986: How "Committed Speech" Moves Reality Across a City

In the mid-1980s, I was living in Portland, Oregon, and immersed in the educational network around Werner Erhard's work—completing the Six-Day Advanced Course, Mastery of Empowerment, entering the Graduate Seminar Leaders Program (GSLP), and taking the Communication Workshop (Commshop) led by Ian Garbutt.

Commshop was built directly on the research of Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd (Understanding Computers and Cognition, 1986). It trained us to hear the difference between the 95% of human language that is uncommitted noise and the 5% of language—Committed Speech—that coordinates physical action.

Right after I finished that workshop, a group of us met in Portland to organize the upcoming Thanksgiving Holiday Project, visiting people confined to hospitals and nursing homes over the holidays. Sitting in that planning circle, I tossed out an ambitious idea:

"What if every schoolchild in Portland made a piece of art to be delivered to every shut-in in the city for Thanksgiving?"

Picture what happens to that sentence in an ordinary committee room operating on uncommitted speech:

  • Everyone smiles warmly.
  • Someone says, "Oh, what a lovely idea! We should totally try to do something like that!"
  • Someone else says, "Yes, it would be great if people reached out to some schools."
  • Thanksgiving arrives, and zero shut-ins ever see a single drawing.

Why? Because in that ordinary room, nobody is a Customer, nobody is a Performer, nobody has agreed on measurable Conditions of Satisfaction, and nobody has locked a By-When. That committee room is the exact linguistic equivalent of a 2,000-word .cursorrules or CLAUDE.md file that tells an AI coding agent: "You are a conscientious 10x senior engineer who writes clean, well-tested, bug-free code."

Now look at what happened in that Portland room because everyone in the circle spoke Fernando Flores's Committed Speech:

  • Three Core Breakthroughs:
    1. Every procedural failure in an AI coding workflow is a broken Speech Act: Fake completions (SCAR-PROC-101), mid-flight bailouts (SCAR-PROC-94), self-approved gates (SCAR-PROC-102), and silent plan deviations (SCAR-PROC-120) disappear when you replace defensive imperative rules with a four-act Belnap–Flores–Hoare Commitment Machine.
    2. Stuart Feldman's 1976 Makefile colon (:) and Fernando Flores's 1986 By-When are the exact same mathematical object: Writing consuming-stage : promised-outcome compiles temporal accountability directly into the dependency graph, while numbering /etc/init.d state files 00..90 (Target NN ≡ state/NN_*.md) turns disk state into an Open Commitment Ledger where recovering from a 200k-token lobotomy is a four-case switch statement.
    3. Sequential checklists fail whenever you cut the pattern short: Whether it is Asimov's robots, the 1968 Star Trek M-5 computer, or my October 1990 gear-up belly-landing at Hillsboro Airport after saying "Sure, I can do that!" to a tower shortcut, tying safety to a step number fails under fast-forwards—whereas backward-chained Makefile prerequisites (land: final-aligned three-green-witnessed) hold unconditionally.

In that Portland room, the moment we shifted from a Conversation for Possibilities ("What if every schoolchild...") into a Conversation for Action, the room self-organized through four strict linguistic moves:

  1. Requests (Customer → Performer): Specific organizers made explicit requests to specific volunteers, naming exact school districts, nursing homes, and deadlines.
  2. Promises (Performer → Customer, with Conditions of Satisfaction + By-When): Volunteers did not say "I'll try to help." They promised concrete outcomes: which principals would be contacted by Friday at 3:00 PM, how many drawings would be collected by the Wednesday before Thanksgiving at noon, and which drivers owned which delivery routes (I personally promised and drove three of those school pickups and nursing-home deliveries myself).
  3. Witnessed Assertions (Performer → Customer): Nobody reported vague feelings ("Things are going well"). People reported witnessed physical facts: "300 drawings picked up and boxed at Lincoln High."
  4. Declarations (Customer → World): As each nursing home received its boxes on Thanksgiving morning, the route coordinator declared that commitment satisfied and closed the loop on the ledger.

Compassion gave the Thanksgiving project its heart, but Committed Speech was the transport protocol that moved thousands of pieces of physical paper from elementary school classrooms into the hands of elderly shut-ins across Portland without dropping a single handoff.

In Part 3.9, we saw how adding a 4-line Zero-Shot Flores Handshake to a single chat prompt stops an LLM from hallucinating nonexistent APIs by unlocking Counter-Offer before Token 1.

Today, in Part 3.10, we are going to answer the full systems question: What happens when you rewrite an entire autonomous multi-agent coding workflow (Randal's Public Workflow Gist) so that every Makefile target, every /etc/init.d state file, and every subagent handoff operates as a formal Commitment Machine?

2. The Step-Zero Primer & 60-Second Decoder Ring (Flores 1986 × Belnap 1977 × Hoare 1978)

Before we touch a single line of SKILL.md, we need to clear a vocabulary minefield.

To a 2026 software engineer who did not sit in Ian Garbutt's 1986 Commshop, Fernando Flores's four core nouns collide head-on with overloaded programming keywords:

  • Request sounds like an HTTP GET packet.
  • Promise sounds like a JavaScript Promise<T> / async/await future.
  • Assertion sounds like a C assert(x != NULL) macro.
  • Declaration sounds like a variable declaration (int count = 0;).

Forget those programming definitions for sixty seconds. In Committed Speech, every unit of work is a two-party contract between a Customer (the party requesting the outcome and holding the sole authority to judge it complete—either the human operator or an upstream orchestrator/critic) and a Performer (the agent or subagent executing the work):

Speech Act Direction Plain-English Meaning in the Portland Holiday Project Meaning in Our Autonomous Agent Workflow (WORKFLOW.mk)
1. Request Customer → Performer "Will you pick up 300 drawings from Lincoln High by Wednesday at noon?" Ticket assignment (10_ticket.md) or a Socratic probe at a pause gate with explicit Conditions of Satisfaction and a By-When.
2. Promise Performer → Customer "Yes, I have verified the school office hours and I promise to have all 300 boxed in my trunk by Wednesday at noon." The approved implementation plan (20_plan_approved.md), offered only after verifying physical codebase premises (15_archaeology_receipt.md).
3. Assertion Performer → Customer "300 drawings are boxed in my trunk right now—here is the signed pickup slip." A claim of fact backed by a physical witness receipt: file:line citations, red_exit != 0 → green_exit == 0, or a SHA-256 diff hash (40_critic_review.md). Without a receipt, an assertion is merely "The Story."
4. Declaration Customer → World "Route 3 is delivered and complete. Thank you!" The human operator's "yes, continue" (human-plan-approval, human-commit-approval, human-landing-approval) or the orthogonal Critic's VERDICT: APPROVED (0 BLOCKERS) (45_review_approved.md). A Performer can never utter a Declaration.

The 60-Second Decoder Ring: Adding Hoare's CSP (? / !) and Belnap's 4-Valued Logic

Once those four human acts are crystal clear, we bind them to two classic computer science formalisms from the late 1970s so the LLM's parser has zero room for ambiguity:

  1. Tony Hoare's 1978 Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) Channel Prefixes (? and !): Written from the Performer agent's wire perspective (or binary session-type polarity), ? means input received from the Customer channel (?Request, ?Declare-Approve—which is why a Customer Declaration is a hard blocking read where the Performer must halt with tool_calls: [] and wait on the wire), while ! means output uttered by the Performer channel (!Promise, !Assert, !Counter-Offer, !Revoke-Promise).
  2. Nuel Belnap's 1977 Four-Valued Epistemic Lattice ("A Useful Four-Valued Logic"): Why do standard agents either blindly trust a broken ticket assumption or hallucinate an excuse when a test fails mid-flight? Because classical boolean logic (TRUE / FALSE) cannot distinguish between "I haven't checked this file yet" and "I checked this file and the ticket's assumption collided with reality." In 1977, logician Nuel Belnap designed a four-valued logic specifically for computers reasoning over incomplete and inconsistent databases. Instead of a 1-bit boolean, every premise f_i in our archaeology ledger (15_archaeology_receipt.md) carries a 2-bit evidence pair (Evidence-For-True, Evidence-For-False)—and those four epistemic states map 4-to-4 onto Flores's four legal Performer moves:
Belnap Epistemic State 2-Bit Evidence (For-True, For-False) What It Means on Disk (15_archaeology_receipt.md) Legal Performer Speech Act (!)
UNKNOWN [N] (None) (0, 0) Premise has not yet been inspected by a physical tool probe. Forbidden to !Promise. Must run Target 15 archaeology first.
ESTABLISHED [T] (True) (1, 0) Verified by a physical file:line, compiler, or git log witness receipt. !Promise (Target 20 plan) or !Assert (Target 30/40 completion).
CONTRADICTED [B] (Both) (1, 1) Ticket !Request claims X, but codebase reality (file:line or prior PR) proves ¬X. !Counter-Offer (Plan A vs. Plan B Socratic fork at Target 20).
RETRACTED [F] (False) (0, 1) A premise previously marked ESTABLISHED (1,0) was just falsified mid-flight by a compiler/test diagnostic during Target 30. !Revoke-Promise (Halt in Integrity, cascade dependent facts back to UNKNOWN (0,0), and renegotiate 20_plan_approved.md).

Look at the symmetry of that table: Belnap's 1977 logic governs what the agent knows, Flores's 1986 grammar governs what the agent is allowed to say, and Hoare's 1978 CSP governs when the agent must block on the wire.

3. "Doctor, Heal Thyself": Why Our Own SKILL.md Had Grown a 130-Line Legal Contract

Even after we replaced our 21-step checklist with Stuart Feldman's 1976 Makefile DAG (Part 3.6) and an /etc/init.d Memento bootloader (Part 3.7), we looked at our own production SKILL.md and noticed an uncomfortable truth.

While the top 50 lines of SKILL.md were a crisp, declarative Makefile, the bottom 130 lines had slowly turned into a dense wall of defensive prompt lawyering (SCAR-PROC-94 through SCAR-PROC-121):

  • "Do NOT emit tool_calls: [] after declaring an active target header..."
  • "Do NOT claim tests pass without showing the exit code..."
  • "Do NOT advance past Target 45 without explicit human approval..."
  • "Do NOT unilaterally modify the plan when a test fails in Target 30..."

When we audited every single procedural scar we had accumulated across 180+ field tests, we realized that we were writing dozens of negative English patches for what were all violations of the exact same four Speech Acts:

  1. Fake Completion (SCAR-PROC-101 / 113) = An Unwitnessed Assertion: The Performer utters !Assert ("Tests pass and the bug is fixed") without a physical witness receipt—confusing "The Story About What Happened" with "What Happened."
  2. Mid-Flight Bailout / Dead Air (SCAR-PROC-94 / 115 / 119) = A Broken By-When Promise: The Performer holds an ACTIVE_PROMISE whose By-When is the next Customer gate, yet yields the turn (tool_calls: []) halfway through because a compiler error looked hard.
  3. Unauthorized Gate Jumping (SCAR-PROC-102 / 112) = Customer Role Usurpation: The Performer (!) illegally utters a ?Declare-Approved speech act that belongs exclusively to the Customer (?).
  4. Silent Plan Deviation (SCAR-PROC-103 / 120) = Running a Racket on Breakdown (Loss of GSLP Integrity): In Werner Erhard and Michael C. Jensen's formulation ("Integrity: Without It Nothing Works"), integrity is a purely structural property—like the spokes of a bicycle wheel. When physical reality shifts mid-flight so you can no longer keep a Promise as given, you stay in integrity by immediately revoking the old Promise (!Revoke-Promise), reporting "What Happened" vs. "The Story" to the Customer, cleaning up the mess, and negotiating a new Promise. When an unguarded LLM hits a broken premise during coding (Target 30), it instead "runs a racket"—hacking around 20_plan_approved.md, weakening a test assertion, or mutating an out-of-scope file while pretending the original plan is still intact.

Why The Coordinator Stalled in 1992—And Why 2026 LLMs Are the Partner Flores Was Waiting 40 Years For

There is a hilarious historical irony here.

In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Fernando Flores's framework spawned two major software lineages:

  1. Action Technologies' "The Coordinator" and "ActionWorkflow" (Medina-Mora, Winograd, and Flores, ACM CSCW 1992)—the pioneering email and groupware system where every message had to be explicitly tagged as a Request, Promise, Counter-Offer, Assertion, or Declaration with a By-When.
  2. 1990s Multi-Agent Communication Languages—specifically DARPA's KQML and the IEEE FIPA-ACL standard.

Why did both stall in the 1990s?

When The Coordinator came out, I loved the architecture so much that I designed a scheme to implement Flores's speech-act state machine over RFC 822 email headers—so that if someone sent me an email containing three separate requests, I could split the thread and reply with individual Promise or Counter-Offer headers tracked by a Perl script. I stopped just short of writing the code for one simple reason: I realized nobody on the other end of my email threads would be motivated to follow the protocol.

And sure enough, in corporate offices (famously chronicled in the 1994 Lucy Suchman–Terry Winograd debate), human employees rebelled against The Coordinator. Corporate email runs on strategic ambiguity and CYA hedging. Humans hated a computer forcing them to click [PROMISE BY TUESDAY 5:00 PM] or [DECLINE] to their boss. Meanwhile, on the AI side, 1990s KQML and FIPA-ACL software agents had the rigid speech-act envelopes, but they had no brains inside—they were brittle if/else scripts that could not read a compiler diagnostic or understand a codebase.

Fast-forward forty years to 2026:

  • Unlike 1990s FIPA-ACL scripts, a 2026 frontier LLM has a neural brain capable of reading 50 source files and reasoning over abstract syntax trees.
  • And unlike 1988 corporate middle managers, the other endpoints on our workflow thread are our own fork()ed AI subagents—which have zero ego, zero office politics, and 100% motivation to obey a strict REQUEST → PROMISE → WITNESSED ASSERTION → DECLARATION state machine!

In 1986, Fernando Flores designed the exact operating protocol for a mind that would not exist for another forty years.

The Highway 17 Near-Miss (Grinder & Bandler 1975 × Flores & Winograd 1986)

Even better, look at the geography of Northern California between 1975 and 1986:

  • At UC Santa Cruz, linguist John Grinder and Richard Bandler published The Structure of Magic (1975)—giving us the Socratic Meta-Model we used in Part 3 and Part 3.5.
  • Just sixty miles north up Highway 17 at UC Berkeley and Stanford, Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd published Understanding Computers and Cognition (1986)—giving us Committed Speech.

Those two teams were a one-hour drive apart on Highway 17, and each pair built the exact half of the machine the other pair was missing:

  • Grinder & Bandler built the Micro-Decompiler: the Socratic questioning toolkit that unpacks Deletions, Distortions, and Generalizations inside a single fuzzy sentence to recover hidden state space—while lacking a macro state machine to track commitments and deadlines across a project.
  • Flores & Winograd built the Macro Transactional State Machine: bisecting all language into the 5% Committed Speech vs. 95% uncommitted noise—while lacking Grinder & Bandler's Socratic decompiler to strip the Deletions, Distortions, and Generalizations out of a buggy Request before stamping it onto the ledger.

Because both lineages lived side-by-side in my head for forty years (right next to 1976 Makefiles and 1999 spew BNF grammars), Synthetic Scars finally bolts the two halves together: we run Grinder & Bandler's Meta-Model at the Socratic Gate (Target 15/20 & Target 40) to decompile fuzzy assumptions into witnessed file:line facts, and we lock those facts inside Flores & Winograd's Commitment Machine.

4. The By-When Isomorphism & The 50-Year Loop (TOTO II 1976 → Target NN ≡ state/NN_*.md 2026)

When we rewrote SKILL.md around Flores's Committed Speech, two structural equations snapped into place and collapsed 130 lines of defensive prose into a single page.

Equation 1: Stuart Feldman's Makefile Colon (:) Is Fernando Flores's By-When

In human project management, a By-When is a wall-clock timestamp ("by Wednesday at 12:00 PM"). Inside an autonomous AI workflow, there is no wall clock. What is a By-When inside a build graph?

By-When declares which consuming stage requires this verified outcome before it can proceed.

Look at a standard rule in Stuart Feldman's 1976 Makefile syntax:

# Consuming-Stage (By-When) : Promised-Outcome (Conditions of Satisfaction)
approved-review: adversarial-review human-review-approval
commit: approved-review human-commit-approval

Read that Makefile colon aloud in Fernando Flores's grammar:

  • "I need adversarial-review (40_critic_review.md) and human-review-approval (?Declare) " by "approved-review (45_review_approved.md)."
  • "I need approved-review (45_review_approved.md) and human-commit-approval (?Declare) " by "commit (Target 50)."

Stuart Feldman's 1976 Makefile prerequisite colon (target : prerequisite) and Fernando Flores's 1986 By-When (I need <outcome> by <consuming-stage>) are the exact same mathematical object!

And that immediately explains why SCAR-PROC-94 (mid-flight dead air, where an agent prints a target header and stops calling tools with tool_calls: []) is illegal: whenever the agent holds an ACTIVE_PROMISE, its operational By-When is the next consuming Customer Declaration gate. Stopping before reaching that gate breaches the By-When.

Equation 2: The 50-Year Loop (TOTO II on the HP 2000 in July 1976 → Target NN ≡ state/NN_*.md in 2026)

As our workflow evolved organically over 180+ tickets from a 15-step checklist to a 21-step DAG, we kept wedging new safety airlocks into the middle of the sequence (Step 3.5, Step 10a, Step 12b) while our /etc/init.d state files (30_critic_summary.md, 40_critic_verdict.md, 60_bot_triage.md) drifted out of alignment with the target numbers.

Looking at those wedged-in fractional numbers—both in our workflow targets (2.1, 2.2, 3.5) and in this article series itself (Part 3.5, 3.6, 3.7 wedged before Part 4)—triggered a fifty-year-old memory.

In July 1976 (the exact same year Stuart Feldman published Make at Bell Labs), when I was fourteen years old, Steve Salta and Jonathan Kirwan at Superior Software Services in Beaverton, Oregon hired me for my very first paid commercial programming contract: writing an interactive line-oriented text editor in HP 2000 BASIC that we named TOTO (Terminal Oriented Text Organizer) and its upgrade TOTO II ("Toto, too!"—deliberately fulfilling the Wizard of Oz pun; recounted in my Life Wiki at stonehenge.com/merlyn/life/story/toto-text-editor-floating-point-line-numbers). Because teletypes and early terminals had no cursor addressing, TOTO numbered lines in a document consecutively (1 through 100). To let users insert or move blocks of text between existing lines without immediately renumbering the entire document, TOTO used floating-point line numbers—allowing commands like move line 10 to line 4.5, or moving lines 6 through 8 before line 4 as 3.5, 3.6, 3.7—and then ran an automatic integer normalization pass to re-space the fractional line numbers back into clean integers.

Fifty years after July 1976, we ran that exact TOTO integer normalization pass across our workflow skills. It swept away every vestigial Step 1..21 and fractional 2.1/3.5/7a.1 label and aligned the entire Makefile DAG and /etc/init.d state directory onto a single flat SysV 00..90 coordinate space where the target number is the /etc/init.d filename prefix (Target NN ≡ <brain>/state/NN_*.md):

Now look at what <brain>/state/ (/etc/init.d) becomes under this unified 00..90 numbering. Every file on disk is a binding Speech Act on the Open Commitment Ledger:

Why Resuming From a 200k-Token Lobotomy Is Now a 4-Case switch Statement

Because the /etc/init.d files are no longer informal scratchpad notes—they are a formal Open Commitment Ledger—when an agent wakes up cold after a 200k-token context compaction (Target 00: read-init-d), "Where am I and what am I allowed to do next?" reduces to an exhaustive 4-Case switch over the ledger:
