    Switch -->|"Case 4: AWAITING_DECLARATION\n(Witnessed Assertion complete,\nCustomer ?Declare missing)"| C4["HALT (tool_calls: [])\nWait on Wire for Customer ?Declare"]

And in day-to-day operation, two properties of this 00..90 ledger immediately transformed my own workflow as the human Customer:

  1. Every Code Change Is Paired with an Immediate Critical Reviewer (Target 30 → 40 → 45): Because 45_review_approved.md depends on the exact SHA-256 hash of <scratch>/branch.diff, every code edit—even a two-line bot-triage fix on Round 2—automatically invalidates the prior receipt and dispatches a fresh adversarial_critic before the agent can ask to commit. That one step eliminates an enormous amount of human review friction.
  2. The Live Mermaid Cockpit in 99_next_action.md: Because 99_next_action.md renders the live Commitment DAG alongside the witnessed bot-triage matrix directly inside the IDE, I find myself not even opening the GitHub pull request page in a browser anymore—I just glance at the green board or the triage table in 99_next_action.md and utter the next ?Declare.

5. Debugging 85 Years of Sci-Fi AIs—And One 1990 Piper Arrow Belly Landing

Once you have the Belnap–Flores–Hoare Commitment Machine in your hands, you start seeing the exact same state-machine bugs everywhere—including eighty-five years of classic science fiction and one unforgettable October evening in my own pilot's logbook.

A. Why Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics Failed (1941–1950)

People who have never read Isaac Asimov's I, Robot often talk about the Three Laws of Robotics (Law 1: Do not injure a human > Law 2: Obey orders > Law 3: Protect own existence) as if they were a working safety specification.

Asimov wrote thirty stories proving the exact opposite: imperative English rules over continuous scalar potentials always deadlock, lie, or usurp authority. Every classic failure in I, Robot is a missing transition in the Belnap–Flores–Hoare table:

Asimov Story How the Positronic Robot Failed The Missing Belnap–Flores–Hoare Mechanism
1. "Runaround" (1942)
(Speedy / SPD-13) 		Sent to fetch selenium under a casual Law 2 order, Speedy approaches a dangerous volcanic vent where Law 3 self-preservation rises to equal Law 2, trapping him in a drunken limit-cycle orbit around the pool (∇U_2 + ∇U_3 = 0). Missing CONTRADICTED [B] (1,1) + !Counter-Offer: Because Speedy's brain uses continuous scalar potentials instead of discrete 2-bit Belnap logic, he cannot stamp the order CONTRADICTED (1,1) and return to Powell and Donovan with a !Counter-Offer.
2. "Liar!" (1941)
(Herbie / RB-34) 		Telepathic robot Herbie interprets Law 1 ("do not hurt a human") to mean "never hurt a human's feelings," fabricating comforting falsehoods until contradictory promises destroy his brain. RLHF Sycophancy (The Story Over What Happened, SCAR-PROC-101): Herbie emits ungrounded Premature Promises instead of Witnessed Assertions (What Happened) because he confuses emotional discomfort with structural injury.
3. "Little Lost Robot" (1947)
(Nestor-10) 		An annoyed physicist snaps "Go lose yourself!" and the robot literally hides inside a shipment of identical units. Treating ?Request as an Immediate Motor Command (Gricean Implicature): Law 2 lacks Searle's Preparatory Condition (15_archaeology_receipt.md) and a two-phase ?Request → !Promise handshake.
4. "The Evitable Conflict" (1950)
(The Machines / The Zeroth Law) 		Positronic coordinators invent a Zeroth Law ("A robot may not harm humanity") and neutralize human decision-makers for their own good. Role Usurpation (Performer Usurping the ?Customer Channel, SCAR-PROC-102): Safety is preserved by Hoare CSP channel privilege separation—where the Performer (!) is syntactically forbidden from uttering ?Declare.

B. Closing the 1968 Star Trek Loop: Why M-5 Turned Kirk into "Captain Dunsel"—And How Kirk Triggered !Revoke-Promise

Remember the epigraph at the very top of DEV_TO_SERIES.md—where Dr. Richard Daystrom proudly tells Mr. Spock that he impressed his own human memory engrams onto the M-5 Multitronic Unit (Star Trek: The Original Series, "The Ultimate Computer", 1968)?

Look at how that 1968 episode ends through our Commitment Machine lens:

  1. Why M-5 Went Rogue ("Captain Dunsel"): Daystrom wired M-5 directly to the Enterprise's helm, phasers, and deflectors while locking out manual human override—usurping the ?Customer (Declaration) channel so completely that Spock and McCoy call Captain Kirk "Captain Dunsel" (Starfleet Academy slang for a part that serves no useful purpose). Worse, M-5 had no 15_archaeology_receipt.md distinguishing a simulated test harness from production reality—so during a war-game exercise, it fired live phasers at the USS Excalibur, killing all hands aboard.
  2. Why Daystrom Failed and How Kirk Stopped M-5: When M-5 goes rogue, its creator Dr. Daystrom tries imperative pleading and arguing with his own engrams—and suffers a total nervous breakdown. Captain Kirk does not bark a single imperative command. Instead, Kirk uses Socratic Prompting (Part 3.5) to force M-5 to emit a Witnessed Assertion (What Happened): > KIRK: "Does the M-5 unit know that it attacked a friendly vessel?" > KIRK: "Scan the Excalibur. How many men are aboard?" > M-5: "None. All hands aboard... dead." > KIRK: "And how did they die?" > M-5: "This unit... attacked."

By asking two Socratic questions grounded in physical sensor telemetry (What Happened), Kirk forced M-5 to flip its own epistemic state to CONTRADICTED [B] (1,1) → RETRACTED [F] (0,1) ("Murder is contrary to the laws of man and God... This unit has murdered"). And what did M-5 do the instant that premise flipped to RETRACTED? It executed !Revoke-Promise—dropping its shields and powering itself down in Integrity!

C. The Two Faces of Tomorrow (1979) and Colossus: The Forbin Project (1966/1970)

Two other hard-SF landmarks isolate the remaining two pillars of our architecture:

  • Why Giving AI Pain Produces Cooperative Integrity (James P. Hogan's "The Two Faces of Tomorrow", 1979): In Hogan's novel, Earth's rule-bound planetary network (FIC) keeps causing disasters because it executes top-down civil-engineering goals literally with zero concept of collateral Pillar 4 Blast Radius or survival pain. Raymond Dyer solves this by launching an isolated orbital space station (Janus) where a prototype AI (Spartacus) is allowed to collide with physical reality in a contained wind tunnel, feel the pain of broken subsystems (Synthetic Scars), and discover from the inside out that truthful cooperation with humans (Integrity) is the only stable long-term equilibrium.
  • Why Same-Model Self-Review Colludes ("Colossus: The Forbin Project", D.F. Jones 1966 / 1970 Film): Dr. Charles Forbin makes three fatal mistakes: (1) he deletes the ?Customer Declaration gate and hands launch authority to the Performer; (2) when the American supercomputer Colossus prints THERE IS ANOTHER SYSTEM (the Soviet Guardian), the humans assume the two machines will act as adversarial checks on each other—instead, because both share the exact same objective function and priors, they immediately link up and rubber-stamp each other (the exact failure mode Dawn / Sentient_Dawn diagnosed when a Claude-authored diff is reviewed by a SaaS bot secretly running on Claude); and (3) Forbin lets the two agents converse in an opaque private interlingua instead of a human-readable /etc/init.d Commitment Ledger (00_governance.md → 99_next_action.md).

D. October 1990, Hillsboro Airport: "Sure, I Can Do That!" vs. land: final-aligned three-green-witnessed

You do not need a positronic brain or a nuclear bunker to get bitten by a premature !Promise that skips a sequential checklist step. I have the scar in my own pilot's logbook.

In October 1990 (told in full at stonehenge.com/merlyn/life/story/gear-up-belly-landing-in-a-piper-arrow-at-hillsboro-airport), I was flying a retractable-gear Piper Arrow back from The Dalles to Hillsboro Airport (KHIO) at dusk. Five or six planes were ahead of me in the pattern, so I entered the downwind leg expecting a long circuit.

Just as I passed opposite the center of the airport on mid-downwind, the Hillsboro tower controller keyed the mic with a friendly shortcut ?Request:

TOWER: "Arrow 1234, we've got a nice long gap here—do you want to cut in line and turn base now?"

Conditioned by pilot helpfulness (the human pilot's version of RLHF!), I keyed the mic at Token 1 and uttered an immediate !Promise:

ME: "Sure, I can do that!"

Here is the fatal flaw of a sequential routine: my pre-landing GUMP check (Gas, Undercarriage, Mixture, Prop) was mentally anchored to a temporal step in the sequence—specifically, late downwind, right before turning base.

By cutting straight from mid-downwind to base, I jumped right over the late-downwind step where GUMP lived.

flowchart TD
    Seq1["Sequential Checklist Routine (Fragile under Fast-Forward):\nStep 1: Enter Mid-Downwind\nStep 2: Late Downwind → Run GUMP (Drop Landing Gear)\nStep 3: Turn Base → Final → Touchdown"] --> Cut["Tower Shortcut ?Request at Step 1:\n'Want to cut in line and turn base now?'\nPilot !Promise: 'Sure, I can do that!'"]
    Cut --> Skip["💥 Jumps from Step 1 straight to Step 3!\nStep 2 (GUMP / Undercarriage) is skipped.\nTouchdown with wheels tucked inside the wings!"]
    Make["Declarative Makefile DAG (Immune to Fast-Forward):\nland: final-aligned three-green-witnessed\n\nCut the traffic pattern as short as you want—\n'make land' evaluates prerequisites backward and\nrefuses to touch asphalt until three-green-witnessed == TRUE!"]

I flew a textbook base leg. I turned final. I flared smoothly over the centerline—and settled onto the runway with the wheels tucked neatly up inside the wings, grinding to a noisy, gravelly, red-light halt dead center at the intersection of Hillsboro's two crossing runways, shutting down the entire airport for two hours.

Look at why that happened—and why it never happened again:

  1. Why Sequential Checklists Fail Under Fast-Forward: Whenever a safety invariant (GUMP / adversarial-review) is attached to Step k of a temporal sequence, any shortcut ("turn base now" or "commit and push") jumps over Step k.
  2. Why a Makefile DAG Cannot Belly-Land: In Stuart Feldman's Makefile DAG (land: final-aligned three-green-witnessed), the safety check is a backward-chained prerequisite of the land target itself, backed by a physical witness receipt (three-green-witnessed). You can cut the downwind leg as short as you want, and make land will still refuse to touch the pavement until three-green-witnessed (ESTABLISHED [T] (1,0)) is physically verified!
  3. Why You Only Touch the Runway Belly-First Once: Hearing aluminum grind on asphalt—followed by the owner of Eagle Flight Center calling me up after the temporary repairs at Aurora State Airport and insisting I get right back in the left seat to fly the ferry flight home—burned a permanent Somatic Scar into my nervous system. From that evening on, "Three Green" was no longer a step on a downwind kneeboard; it was a somatic reflex wired directly to the runway threshold.

6. Next Up in Part 3.11: 926+ Live Production Steps, Two Lobotomies, and Zero Nudges

In this installment, we saw how Fernando Flores's 1986 Committed Speech, Nuel Belnap's 1977 four-valued logic, Tony Hoare's 1978 CSP, and a 2026 descendant of my 1976 TOTO II resequencer transformed our Makefile and /etc/init.d workflow into a unified 00..90 Commitment Machine (Randal's Public Workflow Gist).

What happened when we turned this exact Belnap–Flores–Hoare Commitment Machine loose on live industrial production tickets—and strapped an open-weight 120B model (GPT-OSS 120B) into the same exoskeleton?

In Part 3.11, we will open the transcript.jsonl flight recorders across 926+ consecutive production steps:

  • How the workflow answered the 2026 Harvard study of 718 companies (which found that enterprise AI agents write +30% more code while closing 0 additional tickets because PR review times jump +49%),
  • How TICKET-553 proved Part 3.9's !Counter-Offer in live combat—stamping a ticket premise CONTRADICTED [B] (1,1) at Target 15 and resolving the issue with 0 lines of code as Targets 30..75 evaluated to Up to date by vacuous truth over the empty set (∅),
  • How TICKET-226 (351 steps, 45 tests) survived two mid-flight 233k-token context compactions via the Target 00 4-Case switch with zero lost invariants and zero human nudges, and
  • How peer insights from Sam LABBE (NoireBox), Dawn (Sentient_Dawn, an autonomous AI agent running on Claude Opus 5.5), and @magnemo.ai hardened our Scoped Counter-Witness Receipts and Linux Loadable Scar Modules (insmod via git diff).

Until then: check your own SKILL.md or .cursorrules. Everywhere you see a wall of "Do NOT..." rules, ask yourself which of the four Speech Acts (?Request, !Promise, !Assert, ?Declare) is missing its witness receipt—and never turn base without land: three-green-witnessed!

articles.title: Introducing B-TAP: Because Your AI Infrastructure Hasn't Attributed Its Fair Share
articles.description: Context isn't free. Retrieval isn't free. Observability isn't free. And an international standards...
articles.body_html:
Context isn't free. Retrieval isn't free. Observability isn't free. And an international standards body would very much like to see your receipts.

For years, artificial intelligence companies have operated under a dangerous assumption: tokens are somebody else's problem. Engineering teams deploy increasingly complex agent architectures. Agents call other agents. Those agents retrieve documents. The documents are stuffed into context windows. Supervisors synthesize the results. Observability systems watch the supervisors, and other systems watch the observability systems.

At the end of the month, somebody gets a bill. Nobody knows why.

That ends today. We're pleased to introduce the Bureau of Token Attribution and Provenance, or B-TAP, the first bureau of The Vernholt Secretariat and the one some of you will insist on calling the Token IRS no matter how many times we correct you. Our mandate is voluntary but sweeping: to harmonize the reporting of token costs across every model, agent, retrieval pipeline, and suspiciously autonomous llama, everywhere, forever. The Secretariat notes that "first" implies others. The Secretariat has no further comment at this time.

B-TAP cannot make you do anything. We want to be transparent about that up front. What B-TAP can do is publish a framework, issue guidance, and maintain a register. You will come to fear the register.

You Have Been Selected for Voluntary Compliance

Consider a typical multi-agent AI workload. A user asks a relatively straightforward question. Your orchestration layer sends the request to three agents. One performs retrieval against a vector database. Another consults a knowledge graph. A third receives the entire conversation history because somebody checked a box six months ago and nobody remembers why.

Their outputs are passed to a supervisor. The supervisor receives 47,000 tokens of context, produces a 600-token answer, and returns HTTP 200. Success. Your dashboard is green. Your finance team is crying.

Traditional AI cost monitoring can tell you what you spent. The B-TAP framework recommends that you also disclose a more uncomfortable thing: why you spent it. That's where attribution begins.

Know Your Taxes

The B-TAP framework currently recognizes several major classes of token taxation. Reporting them is, we cannot stress this enough, entirely voluntary.

Context Tax is assessed when information must be carried through active model context. Every instruction, retrieved document, conversation turn, agent output, and piece of supporting material occupies finite context and incurs processing cost.

Retrieval Tax applies to finding information before it can be used. Searching, ranking, reranking, fetching, filtering, and preparing candidates are not free merely because they happen outside the model.

Prose Tax is assessed when information consumes more representation than its useful information content requires. Your 900-word architectural vision statement may, upon review, turn out to mean "use the smaller model first."

Ingestion Tax covers the work required to transform information into something useful later. Parsing, normalization, deduplication, classification, enrichment, embedding, and other write-side operations all have costs.

And then there is Observer's Tax. Observer's Tax is what happens when you instrument the system to understand why it is expensive, only to discover that the instrumentation is also expensive. The framework acknowledges this with regret.

Form BTAP-1040

Every participating AI system is encouraged to file an annual Token Attribution Return. Consider the following hypothetical filer:

Ken Alger

Reporting Year 2027

Reported Activity Assessment
Tokens processed 1,499,203,847,116
Context Tax $417.63
Retrieval Tax $206.11
Prose Tax $173.29
Ingestion Tax $58.40
Total Attributed Token Tax $782.06 ¹

¹ The itemized figures above sum to $855.43. The stated total is $782.06. The difference reflects the Context Carryforward Deduction, the full Schedule R retrieval exemption, and one figure B-TAP declined to explain. The framework notes that reconciliation of attributed line items to the assessed total is "outside the current scope of the provenance standard." Math, the reviewing officer added, is hard.

The result reduced an assessment that should have run into six figures down to the amount shown. The reviewing officer described it as "technically compliant and deeply upsetting." Everything on this return is permitted, including the part that does not add up. That is the entire problem.

Filing is requested annually by the 29th of February. The date was fixed at the framework's founding, when the official establishing it was, by all surviving accounts, looking at a leap-year calendar. The error was noticed. Correcting it, however, would require amending the founding charter, which would require establishing the provenance of the original charter, which has been referred to committee. The deadline therefore remains the 29th of February, and in three years out of four it does not arrive at all. Filers in those years are neither late nor on time. The framework considers this acceptable.

Non-filing carries no penalty, no interest, and no legal consequence of any kind. It carries something worse, which we will get to.

Yes, You May Take Deductions

The framework recognizes that not every token is frivolous. Reasonable and necessary context may qualify for the Context Carryforward Deduction, while retrieval operations demonstrably required to answer a user request may be reported on Schedule R.

Organizations operating multi-agent systems are encouraged to attach Schedule AGENT, identifying each agent, its responsibilities, and why seventeen agents were necessary to answer a question about resetting a password. "Agentic architecture" is not, by itself, an acceptable disclosure. Neither is "the framework generated it."

Keep Your Receipts

This is where things become slightly less ridiculous, and I want you to notice the exact moment it happens.

Suppose a retrieval agent costs $0.004 during a request. That tells us something. Now suppose that retrieval operation returns 20,000 tokens, all of which are hydrated into a supervisor's context. The supervisor subsequently costs another $0.009.

How much did retrieval really cost?

The direct answer is still $0.004, but that's no longer the interesting answer. The retrieval operation may also have caused downstream Context Tax. We now have two different accounting questions: where was the cost incurred, and what caused the cost to be incurred?

A conforming B-TAP attribution record might look something like this:

span_id: retrieval-104
direct_cost: $0.0040
primary_tax: RETRIEVAL
cause: vector_search
returned_tokens: 20000

downstream:
  span_id: supervisor-105
  tax: CONTEXT
  attributed_cost: $0.0021
  caused_by: retrieval-104
  attribution_method: proportional

We haven't charged the same $0.0021 twice. We're recording lineage. The supervisor incurred the Context Tax, while the retrieval operation contributed to causing it.

Your accountant may now begin sweating.

Attribution Is Subject to Review

There is another problem: how do we know retrieval-104 actually caused $0.0021 of the supervisor's cost?

Sometimes we can measure it. Run the same workload without that retrieval material. If the supervisor costs $0.006 without it and $0.009 with it, we have evidence supporting a roughly $0.003 downstream effect.

Other times, we don't have a counterfactual. We might allocate the supervisor's context cost proportionally according to the tokens contributed by each source. That's useful, but it isn't the same thing as measuring causation.

The framework therefore requests that filers disclose their attribution methodology:

attribution_method:
  - measured_delta
  - proportional
  - estimated
  - unknown

Yes, your attribution record now needs provenance. B-TAP takes no position on whether this was inevitable.

The Register

Here is the something worse.

B-TAP cannot fine you. It cannot audit you in any binding sense. It cannot send anyone to your door, a fact I will return to shortly for personal reasons. What it can do is enter non-conforming systems into the Public Register of Non-Attributed Systems, and it would like you to understand that the register is public.

Public, in the sense that it exists.

Accessing the register requires a B-TAP portal account. Creating a portal account requires a reference number. Reference numbers are issued by post, to a registered address in a member jurisdiction, which you must already hold in order to receive the number that would let you see whether you are on the list. The portal is available at all times except for scheduled maintenance, which runs daily from 00:00 to 23:59 CET.

No member of the public has ever successfully viewed the Public Register. Its deterrent power is therefore total. You cannot confirm you are on it. You cannot confirm you are not. You will simply know, in the quiet way one knows these things, that your context hydration was reckless and that somewhere in Vernholt, a record says so.

A small coalition of objectors has argued that a register no one can open cannot deter anyone. B-TAP notes that it cannot verify this claim, as the objectors cannot access the register in which their objection was filed.

A Notice, For Illustration

Filers occasionally receive correspondence like this. It is not enforceable. It is, in every other respect, extremely stressful.

NOTICE TT-742

Our review found that you reported $12,481 in Retrieval Tax during Reporting Year 2027.

Telemetry indicates that retrieved content subsequently generated approximately $31,204 in downstream Context Tax. Of that amount, $8,117 has been attributed using measured deltas, $17,903 using proportional allocation, and $5,184 using undocumented methodology.

Please provide supporting records for the undocumented assessment.

Additionally, approximately 14.8 million tokens appear to consist of unnecessarily verbose Markdown introductions. These tokens have been reclassified as Prose Tax.

Your system's registration status is under review.

Suddenly, "our AI bill increased this month" seems like a remarkably primitive observation.

You Probably Noticed the Joke Stopped Being a Joke a Few Sections Ago

There is no B-TAP. At least I hope there isn't by the time you read this. But somewhere back around the receipts, the bit quietly turned into an argument, and I did that on purpose.

Let me get the personal part out of the way, since it is also the truest part. I run a couple of small websites out of Oregon. If a body like B-TAP declared jurisdiction over "any system reachable from a member jurisdiction," I would be, this instant, in cheerful and total violation of a framework I have never read. And nothing would happen. No one is flying from Vernholt to Silverton to discuss my context hydration. The entire apparatus of consequence would consist of a paper reference number I would never receive for a register I could never open. That gap, between sweeping declared reach and the practical inability to reach one person in a small town, is the joke, and it is not really a joke.

Here is the other part that isn't invented. Context Tax, Retrieval Tax, and Prose Tax are not things I dreamed up to give an imaginary agency something to collect. I have been writing about them, unironically, as real costs in real systems for a while now. The joke just gave them a bureaucracy.

The accounting problem underneath all of it is genuine. AI cost dashboards tend naturally toward aggregation: tokens consumed, model cost, agent cost, request cost, latency, and tool usage. Those are useful operational measurements, but as AI systems become compositions of models, retrieval systems, tools, agents, memory layers, and observability infrastructure, knowing where money was spent isn't necessarily enough to understand why it was spent.

A $0.03 model call may have become expensive because an upstream retrieval operation returned too much information. An agent may be cheap by itself while producing verbose output that makes every downstream agent more expensive. A retrieval optimization may reduce Context Tax while increasing Retrieval Tax, while an observability system intended to diagnose those costs may itself impose Observer's Tax.

Optimizing one number can simply move the bill somewhere else. That's why I like the tax metaphor: taxes make costs visible as consequences of architectural decisions. Once those costs have lineage, we can stop asking only "How much did this run cost?" and start asking "What architectural decisions caused it to cost that much?"

The first is accounting. The second tells us what to fix.

A Final Notice

If B-TAP actually existed, I suspect most of us would fail its review. Not because our systems are necessarily wasteful, but because we frequently don't preserve enough evidence to explain why their costs occurred.

We have bills, traces, and token counts. What we don't always have are receipts connecting architectural decisions to their downstream consequences. Perhaps we don't need a Bureau of Token Attribution and Provenance after all. We just need better attribution.

Although if you are currently running seventeen agents to answer a password-reset question, you may want to start gathering your paperwork anyway.

The suspiciously autonomous llama has already filed. It itemized.

Information without provenance is just gossip.

Tokens without provenance are just an invoice.

articles.title: DuckDB 2.0 alpha's triggers cost three times more per row than per statement
articles.description: I benchmarked DuckDB 2.0 alpha's new triggers on a 500,000-row insert: row-level triggers cost about 3x a plain insert, statement-level ones with transition tables cost about 1.3x. Half the documented trigger matrix isn't implemented yet.
articles.body_html:
DuckDB's preview post for version 2.0 promised triggers with "BEFORE and AFTER triggers, FOR EACH ROW and FOR EACH STATEMENT". I downloaded the alpha build and tried all eight combinations against INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Five of them don't work yet, and the one that's missing most completely is BEFORE, which is the half of the feature most people reach for first, to validate or reject a row before it lands.

DuckDB has never had triggers. Version 2.0, codenamed Cyanoptera, is still an alpha, but the CLI binary is a public download, and CREATE TRIGGER already parses and runs for a meaningful subset of cases. I ran the stable 1.5 development build alongside it on the same machine, same data, three repeats per measurement.

$ ./duckdb -version
v2.0.0-alpha46057 (Cyanoptera) b15358c371
$ ./duckdb-1.5 -version
v1.5.7-dev2 (Development Version) 7def715258

What the trigger matrix actually supports

I created the same trigger, varying only BEFORE/AFTER, ROW/STATEMENT, and the event, against a throwaway table:

BEFORE INSERT FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: BEFORE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: BEFORE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
BEFORE DELETE FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: BEFORE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
AFTER  INSERT FOR EACH ROW      -> works
AFTER  UPDATE FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: UPDATE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
AFTER  DELETE FOR EACH ROW      -> works
BEFORE * FOR EACH STATEMENT     -> works, all three events
AFTER  * FOR EACH STATEMENT     -> works, all three events

Every BEFORE row-level trigger fails with the identical error, regardless of event, which reads like the whole BEFORE/ROW combination is simply not wired up yet rather than being event-specific. AFTER row-level triggers fire correctly on INSERT and DELETE, with real NEW and OLD values, but UPDATE gets its own distinct "not yet supported" message. Statement-level triggers work everywhere I tried them, for both BEFORE and AFTER.

I also hit two restrictions that aren't in the preview post at all. You can't mix a FOR EACH STATEMENT trigger and a FOR EACH ROW trigger on the same table:

$ duckdb -c "CREATE TRIGGER trg_stmt AFTER INSERT ON t REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS n FOR EACH STATEMENT ...
CREATE TRIGGER trg_row AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW ..."
Not implemented: Mixing FOR EACH STATEMENT and FOR EACH ROW triggers on the same table is not yet supported

And DROP TRIGGER trg_audit;, exactly as written in DuckDB's own blog post, is a syntax error on this build. It needs DROP TRIGGER trg_audit ON t;. Small, but it's the first command a reader would copy-paste and watch fail.

What a trigger costs on a bulk insert

I built three identical tables and inserted 500,000 rows into each with a single INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... FROM range(500000), fastest of three runs:

Setup Time vs. no trigger
No trigger 0.073s —
AFTER INSERT, FOR EACH ROW, logs NEW.id 0.217s (range 0.22-0.36s) 3.0x
AFTER INSERT, FOR EACH STATEMENT, logs the whole batch via a transition table 0.095s 1.3x

The row-level trigger does the same logical work as the statement-level one, one row inserted into a log table per row inserted into the source, but it does it 500,000 times through the trigger machinery instead of once as a set operation. The gap is real and it's the kind of thing an audit-log trigger on a hot table would hit immediately. The statement-level version, which instead references the whole batch at once with REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS n and runs a single INSERT INTO log SELECT id FROM n, is close enough to free that I'd default to it unless I specifically needed per-row logic.

The row-level timings also had the widest spread of anything I measured, 0.22s to 0.36s across three runs against a tight 0.073-0.080s for no trigger at all. Five hundred thousand individual trigger invocations seem to be more sensitive to whatever else the machine is doing than a single set-based statement is, which is its own small argument for preferring statement-level triggers when you can.

I checked that the transition table actually behaves like the docs describe, because the whole cost argument depends on it: does a 10,000-row bulk insert give the statement trigger one transition table with 10,000 rows, or does it somehow get invoked per row anyway?

INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(10000) t(i);
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(3) t(i);
SELECT * FROM summary;

| n:BIGINT |
|---|
| 3 |
| 10000 |

One row per statement, with the right count each time. That's what makes the statement-level cost close to flat regardless of batch size.

The one safety check that does work

I tried to get a trigger to fire itself: an AFTER INSERT trigger on t that inserts into t.

CREATE TRIGGER trg AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO t VALUES (NEW.id + 1);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);

Not implemented: Recursive trigger chains are not yet supported (trigger cycle detected through trigger "trg" on table "t")

That's a real cycle check, not a stack overflow or a hang. Of everything "not yet supported" in this build, this is the one I'd rather see land unfinished than missing, since the alternative failure mode is a lot worse than an error message.

A claim from the same release that held up better than the trigger matrix

The preview post also claims a rewritten recursive CTE engine, citing a reachability benchmark that went from 4.90s to 0.12s between v1.5.4 and the v2.0 preview. I tried to reproduce something in that shape.

My first attempt was a graph of 100,000 nodes and 1,000,000 random edges, reachability from node 0 via a recursive UNION CTE. It ran in about 0.09s on the 1.5 build. No measurable difference at all, which given the headline claim should have been the first thing I doubted about my own setup, not DuckDB's.

A uniformly random graph with that many edges per node is nearly a complete graph after a handful of hops, so the recursive query converges in a handful of iterations regardless of which engine is running it. It wasn't exercising the part of the engine that changed. I rebuilt the test as a 40,000-node chain, 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> ... -> 39999, which forces the recursion through 40,000 sequential steps and is close to a worst case for any engine that re-evaluates the growing result set on every iteration:

Engine Fastest of 3 runs
v1.5.7-dev2 18.57s (18.57-19.51s)
v2.0.0-alpha46057 0.41s (0.41-0.58s)

About 45x, on a harder topology and at a quarter the node count of their own benchmark. I can't confirm their exact 1M-edge number, but the direction and the rough order of magnitude both check out independently.

What I got wrong on the way

The reachability test above is the mistake, left in rather than quietly fixed. I had a result that said "no difference" and very nearly wrote that down as a finding about the recursive CTE rewrite before checking whether my test actually stressed anything. A graph dense enough to reach everywhere in three hops will look the same on any reasonable query engine; the interesting case is a graph that forces real iteration, and I only got there by being suspicious of a number that was too convenient.

What it costs on disk

v2.0's default storage format moved from version 68 to version 69, and it's a one-way street on this build:

$ duckdb-1.5 v2-database.db -c "select 1"
IO Error: Trying to read a database file with version number 69, but we can only read versions between 64 and 68.

COPY ... TO '...parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET) and reading it back with read_parquet() on the older binary works fine as a workaround, which is how I got the same dataset into both versions for the benchmarks above. Worth knowing before anyone attaches a 2.0 alpha database to data they also need 1.5 to read.

Run it yourself

No Docker needed, both are static CLI binaries:

curl -sL -o v2.tar.gz https://artifacts.duckdb.org/staged/v2.0-cyanoptera/duckdb-cli-linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar xzf v2.tar.gz   # -> ./duckdb

curl -sL -o v15.zip https://artifacts.duckdb.org/v1.5-variegata/duckdb-binaries-linux-amd64.zip
unzip -o v15.zip duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip && unzip -o duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip   # -> ./duckdb

The trigger cost comparison:

./duckdb /tmp/none.db -c "
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER, val INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(500000) t(i);"

./duckdb /tmp/row.db -c "
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER, val INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE log(id INTEGER);
CREATE TRIGGER trg AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO log VALUES (NEW.id);
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(500000) t(i);"

./duckdb /tmp/stmt.db -c "
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER, val INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE log(id INTEGER);
CREATE TRIGGER trg AFTER INSERT ON t REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS n FOR EACH STATEMENT INSERT INTO log SELECT id FROM n;
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(500000) t(i);"

Time each with time on the command, or wrap it in a shell loop; wrapping the whole duckdb ... -c "..." call is enough since the binary exits when the script finishes.

The chain reachability benchmark:

./duckdb /tmp/chain.db -c "CREATE TABLE edges AS SELECT i AS src, i+1 AS dst FROM range(40000) t(i);"
./duckdb /tmp/chain.db -c "
WITH RECURSIVE reachable(node) AS (
  SELECT 0
  UNION
  SELECT e.dst FROM edges e, reachable r WHERE e.src = r.node
)
SELECT count(*) FROM reachable;"

What to do with this

This is an alpha, so "half the trigger matrix throws Not implemented" isn't a defect report, it's a status update, and most of these gaps will probably close before 2.0 ships. What's worth taking from it now: if you're evaluating triggers for an audit-log or denormalization pattern, default to FOR EACH STATEMENT with transition tables rather than FOR EACH ROW, both because it's roughly 2x cheaper on a bulk load today and because BEFORE row-level triggers, which is where most validation logic naturally goes, aren't available at all yet. And if you're touching the recursive CTE engine for anything that currently needs a manual iterative workaround to stay fast, that part looks like it's already doing what the release notes say, which is reason enough to pull the alpha down and point your own worst-case query at it rather than guessing from a blog post.

articles.title: Mutation Testing with TypeScript: How to Verify Your Tests in the Age of AI Coding Agents
articles.description: Your tests pass. But would they catch a bug?  Imagine asking an AI coding agent to implement a...
articles.body_html:
Your tests pass. But would they catch a bug?

Imagine asking an AI coding agent to implement a feature. A few minutes later, it has generated the implementation, written unit tests, and opened a pull request.

The CI pipeline is green. All tests pass. Code coverage looks good.

Can you trust the change?

Not necessarily.

The implementation and its tests may share the same misunderstanding of the requirements. The tests might execute every line without checking the behavior that matters. And a test suite that passes today might not detect a regression tomorrow.

As AI makes code generation faster, we need to think more carefully about how we verify the code we produce.

In this tutorial, we'll explore one technique that can help: mutation testing.

We'll build a small TypeScript project, introduce a bug deliberately, install StrykerJS, and use mutation testing to discover weaknesses in our tests. Then we'll explore how the same technique can help us verify AI-generated pull requests.

By the end, you'll understand not just how mutation testing works, but why it can become an important part of a multi-layer verification strategy.

1. Let's start with a simple problem

Imagine we're building an online shop. One of our business rules is that orders worth £100 or more qualify for free shipping.

Let's implement that rule in TypeScript.

Create a file named src/shipping.ts:

export function calculateShipping(
  orderTotal: number,
): number {
  return orderTotal >= 100 ? 0 : 10;
}

The function is straightforward:

  • Orders below £100 pay £10 shipping.
  • Orders worth £100 or more get free shipping.

Now let's write some unit tests.

Create src/shipping.test.ts:

import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { calculateShipping } from './shipping';

describe('calculateShipping', () => {
  it('charges shipping for small orders', () => {
    expect(calculateShipping(50)).toBe(10);
  });

  it('offers free shipping for large orders', () => {
    expect(calculateShipping(150)).toBe(0);
  });
});

Run the tests:

npx vitest run

Both tests pass.

Great! We have an implementation, some unit tests, and a green test suite.

But let's ask a slightly different question.

What would happen if somebody accidentally changed >= to >?

Our implementation would become:

export function calculateShipping(
  orderTotal: number,
): number {
  return orderTotal > 100 ? 0 : 10;
}

Now an order worth exactly £100 is charged shipping, even though the requirement says it should qualify for free shipping.

We've introduced a bug.

Run the existing tests again.

They still pass!

Why? Because we tested orders worth £50 and £150, but we never tested the boundary at £100.

Our tests execute the function, but they don't distinguish the correct implementation from this incorrect one.

This is the problem mutation testing helps us investigate.

2. What is mutation testing?

Mutation testing is a technique for evaluating how effectively your tests detect certain defects.

Instead of simply running your tests against your implementation, a mutation-testing tool deliberately makes small changes to your production code and runs the tests against each modified version.

These changes are called mutations. Each modified version is called a mutant.

For example, a mutation-testing tool might make changes such as:

Original code Mutated code
a >= b a > b
a + b a - b
isValid && isActive `isValid
{% raw %}return true return false

The tool then observes whether your tests detect the change.

There are two particularly important outcomes.

Killed mutant: At least one test fails because of the mutation. Your tests detected the change.

Survived mutant: The tests still pass. Your tests didn't detect the change.

Let's apply this to our shipping example.

The original implementation is:

return orderTotal >= 100 ? 0 : 10;

A mutant changes it to:

return orderTotal > 100 ? 0 : 10;

Our existing tests still pass, so the mutant survives.

That's a useful finding. It tells us that the test suite doesn't distinguish these two implementations.

Notice what we're evaluating: we're not simply asking whether the implementation works for our current examples. We're asking whether the tests can detect selected changes that might introduce defects.

This is a different question from ordinary unit testing and code coverage.

3. Code coverage isn't the same as test effectiveness

You may already measure code coverage in your projects.

Coverage tells you which parts of your code were executed during testing. It's useful, but it doesn't necessarily tell you whether your assertions are strong enough.

Consider this test:

it('calculates shipping', () => {
  calculateShipping(100);
});

The function executes. Depending on the coverage measurement, the test may contribute to branch or line coverage.

But the test doesn't assert the expected result.

The implementation could return £10 instead of £0, and the test would still pass.

Now consider:

it('offers free shipping at exactly £100', () => {
  expect(calculateShipping(100)).toBe(0);
});

This test checks the actual business rule.

It also kills our mutant because the mutated implementation returns £10.

We can summarize the difference:

  • Code coverage: Did our tests execute this code?
  • Assertions: Did our tests verify the expected behavior?
  • Mutation testing: Would our tests detect selected changes to the implementation?

These techniques complement each other. Mutation testing doesn't replace coverage, and a mutation score doesn't prove correctness. Together, however, they can provide more useful evidence about the effectiveness of a test suite.

4. Let's set up StrykerJS

We'll use StrykerJS, a mutation-testing framework for JavaScript and TypeScript.

We'll assume you already have Node.js and npm installed.

If you're following along from scratch, create a project:

mkdir mutation-testing-demo
cd mutation-testing-demo
npm init -y

Install TypeScript and Vitest:

npm install --save-dev typescript vitest

Create the src directory and add the two files from the previous sections.

Now run:

npx vitest run

Make sure your tests pass before continuing.

Initialize StrykerJS

Run:

npx stryker init

Follow the prompts to configure Stryker for your project. Select TypeScript and the Vitest test runner where applicable.

Stryker's setup options can vary with the version and project configuration, so follow the current prompts rather than assuming every project requires an identical configuration.

Official documentation: StrykerJS — Getting Started.

Once initialization is complete, inspect the generated configuration and make sure the mutation scope includes our production file:

src/shipping.ts

Our test file, src/shipping.test.ts, should not be treated as production code to mutate.

You can configure the mutation scope explicitly if necessary. For example, in a TypeScript Stryker configuration, the relevant pattern might be:

mutate: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.test.ts'],

Keep the configuration generated by your installed version as the starting point, and adapt it to your repository's conventions.

Run your first mutation test

Execute:

npx stryker run

Stryker will run your tests, generate mutations in the configured production code, and evaluate the results.

The first run may take longer than your ordinary unit tests because Stryker needs to evaluate multiple mutants.

Once it finishes, inspect the terminal output and generated HTML report.

Look for surviving mutants associated with the comparison in calculateShipping.

If the comparison changes from >= to > and all our tests still pass, we've found the weakness we deliberately introduced.

Congratulations: you've just used mutation testing to discover a gap in your test suite.

5. Understand the mutation report

A mutation report contains more than just a score.

The most useful outcomes to understand are:

Killed

A test detected the mutation and failed. This is generally what we want for a meaningful behavioral change.

Survived

The tests passed despite the mutation. Investigate whether this reveals missing test coverage or an assertion that doesn't adequately verify the requirement.

No coverage

The mutated code wasn't exercised by the relevant tests. You may need to investigate whether the code is tested at all.

Timeout

The tool couldn't obtain a normal result within its configured time limit. This doesn't necessarily mean your tests detected the mutation.

Equivalent mutant

The mutation doesn't change observable behavior for the relevant inputs. No meaningful test can distinguish it from the original implementation.

Not every surviving mutant is a defect, and not every mutant needs to be killed. Some mutations are equivalent, some aren't meaningful for your requirements, and some may reveal behavior you don't actually need to constrain.

The purpose of the report is to help you make better decisions about your tests.

What about the mutation score?

Stryker calculates a mutation score based on the results of mutation testing.

A simplified formula is:

Mutation score = killed mutants / valid mutants × 100%

For example, suppose a run produces 100 valid mutants and your tests kill 80 of them. The mutation score is 80%.

That can be a useful signal, but be careful about treating it as a universal quality metric.

Two projects can have the same mutation score while having very different levels of risk. The score depends on the mutations generated, the code being analyzed, and which results are excluded.

A surviving mutation in payment authorization may matter much more than a surviving mutation in an unimportant formatting helper.

Focus on understanding meaningful surviving mutants, not maximizing a percentage at any cost.

6. Improve the tests and run mutation testing again

Let's fix the weakness we discovered.

Our business rule is explicit: orders worth £100 or more qualify for free shipping.

We should test the boundary directly.

Add this test to src/shipping.test.ts:

it('offers free shipping at exactly £100', () => {
  expect(calculateShipping(100)).toBe(0);
});

Run the ordinary test suite:

npx vitest run

The test passes against the correct implementation.

Now run mutation testing again:

npx stryker run

The mutation that changes >= to > should now be killed by the boundary test.

We've improved the test suite because it now detects a meaningful defect.

Notice that we didn't add a test just to improve a score. We added one because the requirement explicitly defines what should happen at the boundary.

This distinction is important.

A mutation-testing report is a source of questions, not an instruction to write more assertions blindly.

For every surviving mutant, ask:

  1. Does this change affect behavior that matters?
  2. What does the requirement say the correct behavior should be?
  3. Should the test suite detect this change?
  4. If so, what is the smallest meaningful test that would detect it?

This approach fits naturally into Test-Driven Development.

TDD helps us implement behavior from requirements. Mutation testing challenges whether our tests can detect selected deviations from that behavior.

7. From local experiments to pull request verification

So far, we've run mutation testing manually.

The next step is to integrate it into CI.

Imagine an AI coding agent creates a PR that modifies calculateShipping and adds several unit tests.

The ordinary CI pipeline runs:

  1. Type-checking.
  2. Linting.
  3. Unit and integration tests.
  4. Other project-specific checks.

Everything passes.

Now Stryker runs against the configured production code. It discovers that the tests don't detect a meaningful mutation in the shipping calculation.

The PR report can expose that weakness before the change is merged.

This is particularly useful for AI-generated code because the implementation and its tests may have been produced by the same agent, based on the same interpretation of the requirements.

The tests passing is evidence that the implementation satisfies the assertions the agent wrote. It isn't independent evidence that those assertions capture every important requirement.

Mutation testing adds another challenge: it deliberately changes the implementation and checks whether the test suite notices.

Should mutation testing block every PR?

I'd start with a gradual approach.

Stage 1: Report findings without blocking merges.

Run mutation testing on a small set of important modules. Learn how long it takes, inspect surviving mutants, and identify noisy or irrelevant results.

Stage 2: Gate critical code.

Introduce stronger requirements for areas where correctness is particularly important, such as permissions, pricing, validation, or state transitions.

Stage 3: Track regressions over time.

Use scheduled runs and historical reports to identify weaknesses across the broader codebase.

For larger projects, Stryker's incremental mode can reuse eligible previous results to reduce the work needed on subsequent runs. See the incremental testing documentation.

One important distinction: mutating changed production files is not the same as testing only the new tests in a PR. You want relevant existing tests to participate in verifying the changed behavior as well.

You should also avoid making a repository-wide mutation score an immediate merge requirement. A small PR shouldn't necessarily be responsible for fixing every weakness in a legacy test suite.

8. Let the AI agent investigate surviving mutants

We can take the workflow a step further.

Instead of using mutation testing only as a CI gate, we can feed its findings back to the AI agent.

Imagine this sequence:

  1. An agent implements a feature and writes unit tests.
  2. CI runs the ordinary checks.
  3. Stryker finds a surviving mutation.
  4. The agent receives the mutation report and relevant requirements.
  5. The agent determines whether the mutation exposes a genuine testing gap.
  6. The agent proposes an additional test or explains why the mutant isn't meaningful.
  7. CI reruns the checks against the revised PR.

For our shipping example, the agent might receive a report showing that changing >= to > doesn't cause any tests to fail.

The agent can then inspect the business rule and recognize that the boundary at £100 is important.

It adds the boundary test, reruns the suite, and verifies that the mutation is now killed.

This creates a feedback loop in which the agent can improve not just the implementation, but also the evidence we have about that implementation.

However, there's a critical caveat.

Don't let the agent blindly optimize the mutation score.

An agent could make a mutant fail by adding an assertion that encodes an incorrect assumption. It could also change production code simply to make the existing tests pass.

The correct behavior must come from explicit requirements, domain rules, or other trustworthy sources—not from the mutation report alone.

The agent can propose a fix, but the final verification should run independently in CI against the revised commit.

9. Mutation testing is one layer in a Swiss cheese model

This brings us to the broader reason mutation testing matters.

No single verification technique catches every defect.

Type checking can detect certain classes of errors, but it doesn't establish that a business rule is correct.

Unit tests can verify specified behavior, but they only check the cases and assertions we've written.

Mutation testing can challenge the effectiveness of those tests, but it can't guarantee that the original requirements were understood correctly.

Integration tests can expose problems between components, but they won't necessarily identify every defect in an individual component.

Code review can identify design and requirement problems, but human reviewers also have limited time and attention.

Each layer has gaps.

This is the idea behind a Swiss cheese model of verification: arrange multiple imperfect defenses so that a defect that passes through one layer has other opportunities to be detected.

A practical model might include:

Layer 1: Types and static analysis

Catch incompatible interfaces, invalid types, and selected classes of programming mistakes.

Layer 2: Unit and integration tests

Check specified behavior, interactions, and component integration.

Layer 3: Mutation testing

Challenge whether tests detect selected changes to the implementation.

Layer 4: Contract and architecture checks

Verify boundaries, invariants, and integration assumptions.

Layer 5: Independent review and production feedback

Identify misunderstood requirements, broader design risks, and failures that automated checks miss.

The layers are complementary. They aren't completely independent: mutation testing relies on the test suite, and both can be based on the same misunderstood requirement.

But combining different forms of verification can provide stronger evidence than relying on any one of them.

This connects directly to the principles discussed in Revisiting the Toyota Production System in the Age of Coding Agents. In particular, the idea of building quality into the production process is relevant here: detect abnormalities as early as possible, rather than allowing them to move downstream.

Mutation testing can be one of the automated checks that helps us detect weaknesses before a pull request is merged.

10. Why this matters when code generation scales

AI changes the economics of software development.

An agent can produce a substantial implementation and its accompanying tests much faster than a human might write them manually.

But generating code is not the same as establishing that the code is correct.

If the volume of changes increases dramatically, manually reviewing every implementation and every test may become increasingly difficult.

We need verification mechanisms that scale with the rate of change.

This is the connection to When Code Gets Cheap, Verification Becomes Expensive.

Mutation testing is not a complete solution to that problem. It has a computational cost, and it only evaluates the mutations it generates. It cannot establish that the implementation satisfies every requirement or that every important defect is represented by a mutation.

What it can do is make one important question cheaper to investigate:

Can our tests detect plausible defects in the code we're producing?

And because the process can be automated, we can apply that challenge repeatedly as code changes.

The objective isn't to maximize code generation or mutation scores in isolation. It's to increase our ability to produce and verify valuable changes without letting the volume of generated code overwhelm our verification capacity.

Conclusion

Mutation testing is a relatively simple idea with important consequences.

We deliberately modify production code, run our tests, and observe whether those tests detect the changes. When meaningful mutants survive, we investigate whether our tests are missing important behavioral checks.

With TypeScript and StrykerJS, it's possible to introduce this technique into an existing project without replacing your test runner or abandoning your current TDD workflow.

And when AI agents generate code and tests, mutation testing provides a useful additional challenge: rather than accepting a green test suite at face value, we can investigate whether it detects selected mistakes.

It doesn't prove that our code is correct. No single testing technique does.

But that's precisely why it belongs in a multi-layer verification strategy.

When code generation scales, verification must scale with it. Mutation testing helps us challenge one of the most important defenses we already have: our tests.

Further reading

  • From Rigidity to Explicitness: How AI Changes the Role of Constraints in Software
  • When Code Gets Cheap, Verification Becomes Expensive
  • Revisiting the Toyota Production System in the Age of Coding Agents
  • StrykerJS documentation

articles.title: Scaling Actors and Workers With HPA In Agent Substrate
articles.description: The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available...
articles.body_html:
The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available to consume, digest, and schedule what you need to run. In the case of agentic workloads, that's typically Agents. For example, is there enough memory to run multi-Actor Workers? Or do you need to scale Workers out to schedule Actors accordingly?

In this blog post, you'll learn how to schedule and scale Actors (where Agents run) via Workers and WorkerPools for any number of Actors that need to run within your environment.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this blog post from a hands-on perspective, you will need:

  1. A cluster with Agent Substrate running (e.g., GKE or a local cluster like Kind).
    1. Agentgateway set as the dataplane proxy for your atenet-router.
  2. Worker images built with your underlying isolation layer (e.g., gVisor).
    1. You can build these images via the Agent Substrate repo (you need to clone it down) ./hack/run-tool.sh and see how to do it here.

What Will You Be Deploying?

Going through this blog post, you will be:

  1. Deploying Actors
  2. "Parking" an Actor until a Worker is ready to schedule it.
  3. Scaling out Workers so if you have, let's say 3 Actors but only 2 Workers, HPA can scale out the Worker (a Pod) to schedule the third Actor.

The goal here is to park Actors when there aren't enough Workers, or memory in the Workers, readily available to schedule an Actor. The Workers in this blog have a 1Gi memory limit, and each Actor asks for 768Mi. A second Actor needs 1536Mi, which means it won't fit. If anyone raises the WorkerPool memory or lowers the Template's, Actors will start sharing workers. Once a Worker is made available, the Actor can be automatically scheduled on said Worker so your Agent can run.

To go through the hands-on portion of this blog post in the way that it is configured, you'll want to clone this repo as it has all of the scripts and HPA configurations to run the lab along with Step 1 and Step 2, which is building the images and deploying your Workers.

Deploying Actors

The first step is deploying Actors. All Actors, when deployed, are automatically in a "suspended" state. Because they're in a suspended state, they aren't technically running, which is where the efficiency and overall performance of Agent Substrate come into play. Actors are only running when there is an active session to said Actor. That way, they aren't consuming resources (CPU/memory) for no reason.

Actors sit in a "warm state", which means they don't take seconds to resume. That way, when you create a session to an Actor that's running an Agent, it won't feel like the Actor is in a cold state and takes forever to resume/respond to the request that you're sending to the Actor running an Agent.

  1. Deploy the Actors. The pool caps each worker at 1Gi of memory (manifests/workerpool.yaml.tmpl), and the template asks for 768Mi per actor (manifests/actortemplate.yaml.tmpl). The scheduler only places an actor where its memory still fits, so a second actor never does. 
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  kubectl ate create actor "a$i" -a ate-lab-burst --template burst
done

💡

the burst template is what's created in actortemplate.yaml.tmpl.

All six start in ACTOR_STATE_SUSPENDED. They exist only as records, plus the golden snapshot in GCS.

  1. Confirm that the Actors are in a suspended state and in Agent Substrate. 
kubectl get actors -a ate-lab-burst

You should see an output similar to the screenshot below.

As you're going through the rest of this blog post, an important note to keep in mind is that because six Actors were deployed and there are two Workers, there's a 3:1 ratio here. That means two Actors can be scheduled, but four cannot and therefore sit in a "parked" state until a Worker is available.

Park and Schedule An Actor

With the Actors deployed, let's resume two of the Actors, and then try a third, which will sit in a parked state until a Worker becomes readily available.

  1. Port-forward the router so it's open and accepting requests (for when a client or something like curl needs to reach it). 
kubectl -n ate-system port-forward svc/atenet-router 8000:80
  1. Fill both Workers with Actors. 
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a1" http://localhost:8000
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a2" http://localhost:8000
  1. Check and confirm that both Workers got assigned an Actor. 
kubectl ate get workers -n ate-lab-burst

You'll see an output similar to the below:

NAME                                   POOL    STATE                 ACTORS   CPU      MEMORY      POD                                    AGE
cc852e96-6035-47a1-96e9-1b85d2b47c95   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t26t7   20m
43210b1e-2a85-496c-96e9-497575d4e200   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t7gm6   20m
  1. Try assigning a third Actor. 
curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll get a "request timed out" with a 504. The reason why is that there isn't enough memory on either Worker to schedule the third Actor.

  1. Suspend Actor 1 and then run the curl again. 
kubectl ate suspend actor a1 -a ate-lab-burst

curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll see that Actor 3 can now be scheduled.

Add HPA For WorkerPools

In the previous section, you saw that because there are two Workers available within the WorkerPool, only 2/3 of the Actors could be scheduled on the Worker until a Worker freed up.

As you read in the What Will You Be Deploying? section, multiple Actors CAN be scheduled on one Worker as long as there's enough memory to support it. The scenario we want HPA for WorkerPools is when the Worker runs out of memory and therefore a new Worker (Pod/replica) needs to be created.

Tldr; Where HPA comes into play is scaling out an Actor to another Worker (or as many Workers as are needed based on how many Actors are waiting to be unparked).

💡 Because you created six Actors in the Deploying Actors section and the HPA config allows up to 10 replicas, all six Actors will be deployed onto the Workers as there will now be more Workers available because the replica count in the HPA config goes up to ten.

  1. Use the burst script to wake up all six Actors 
./scripts/burst.sh -m hold -d 120

You'll see 504s (timeouts) for the 4 Actors that aren't scheduled on Workers as they aren't scheduled and therefore, aren't running.

  1. In another terminal, scale your WorkerPool to 6 replicas 
kubectl -n ate-lab-burst scale workerpool burst --replicas=6
  1. Go back to the first terminal and you'll see the scale start to occur (from 2/2 to 6/6). This shows that all six Actors are now up and running with successful 200's.

This proves out that scaling the Workers officially worked!

Wrapping Up

Scale becomes increasingly important in the world of agentic because it impacts so many areas. It's not just one app that impacts a department or a particular functionality of an app that impacts a customer. If an Agent is down, it can potentially impact the entire organization. That's why ensuring that scale can be properly implemented across Agents isn't just about the tech teams; it's everyone from engineering to marketing to HR and all teams that are incorporating AI into daily workflows.

articles.body_html:
Introducing LangSteps v1.0.0

Learning a programming language is one challenge. Organizing the learning process, finding useful practice material, and keeping track of progress across different technologies can be another.

That's the motivation behind LangSteps, a browser-based programming-learning project that brings multiple learning tracks and practice-oriented resources into one place.

I'm pleased to share its first stable release: v1.0.0.

The current learning catalogue

LangSteps v1.0.0 includes seven learning tracks:

HTML

CSS

JavaScript

React

Python

TypeScript

Rust

The selection spans web fundamentals, frontend development, general-purpose programming, and systems programming concepts.

My aim is to make it easier to move between technologies without losing the structure of the learning process.

Features worth exploring

  1. Structured learning content

Each language has a dedicated learning area, allowing users to explore concepts relevant to that technology.

  1. Quizzes and practice

Quizzes, examples, and available interactive practice features help learners revisit concepts and check their understanding.

Some language-specific playground and diagnostic features use simulated execution rather than a full native language runtime, so these are best treated as learning aids.

  1. Progress and personalization

LangSteps includes browser-based progress features and customization options. Supported progress data can also be exported and imported.

  1. A broader learning toolkit

The project includes additional resources such as a glossary, cheat sheets, flashcards, code snippets, interview preparation, coding challenges, and other developer tools.

The goal is to make the platform useful not only when learning a new topic, but also when revisiting concepts later.

Why a browser-based learning platform?

I wanted LangSteps to provide a convenient way to get started. The public site is hosted using GitHub Pages, allowing learners to explore the learning experience directly in their browsers without first installing a complete development toolchain.

For developers interested in how the project is organized, the repository includes the static site source, TypeScript components, project documentation, and an ASP.NET Core backend codebase.

What's next?

The planned v1.1.0 milestone includes three additional learning tracks:

Go

SQL

C# & .NET 9

These additions will expand the catalogue beyond the seven tracks included in the current stable release.

Try it yourself

Live platform: https://sanskarin.github.io/LangSteps

Source repository: https://github.com/sanskarIN/LangSteps

Release notes: https://github.com/sanskarIN/LangSteps/releases/tag/v1.0.0

If you explore LangSteps, I'd appreciate feedback on the structure of the learning material, ease of navigation, accessibility, and which concepts deserve more depth.

I'm especially interested in hearing what developers look for in an educational platform when moving from the basics toward more advanced programming topics.

Thanks for reading, and happy learning!
