}

Step 4: Express Server & MCP Transports (SSE & HTTP)

Now we wire Express, the MCP auth middleware, and the transports together.

Look how clean this is: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk gives us mcpAuthRouter and requireBearerAuth.

Create src/index.ts:

import express from "express";
import dotenv from "dotenv";
import { SSEServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/sse.js";
import { mcpAuthRouter, getOAuthProtectedResourceMetadataUrl } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/auth/router.js";
import { requireBearerAuth } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/auth/middleware/bearerAuth.js";

import { createTaskPulseServer } from "./server.js";
import { TaskPulseOAuthProvider } from "./auth/oauthProvider.js";

dotenv.config();

const app = express();
const PORT = process.env.PORT ? parseInt(process.env.PORT, 10) : 8080;
const issuerUrl = new URL(process.env.APP_URL || `http://localhost:${PORT}`);

app.use(express.json());
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }));

// 1. Initialize our OAuth Provider
const oauthProvider = new TaskPulseOAuthProvider({ issuerUrl });

// 2. Mount standard OAuth 2.1 routes:
// /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource, /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, /authorize, /token, /register
app.use(
  mcpAuthRouter({
    provider: oauthProvider,
    issuerUrl,
    scopesSupported: ["tasks:read", "tasks:write", "projects:admin"],
    resourceName: "TaskPulse Project & Task MCP",
  })
);

// 3. Mount the consent decision receiver
app.post("/authorize/decision", async (req, res) => {
  await oauthProvider.handleConsentDecision(req, res);
});

// 4. Create Bearer Auth Middleware (answers with 401 + WWW-Authenticate header when no token is present)
const bearerAuth = requireBearerAuth({
  verifier: oauthProvider,
  resourceMetadataUrl: getOAuthProtectedResourceMetadataUrl(issuerUrl),
});

// Active SSE Connections
const sseTransports = new Map<string, SSEServerTransport>();

// 5. Protected SSE Stream Endpoint
app.get("/sse", bearerAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const transport = new SSEServerTransport("/messages", res);
  sseTransports.set(transport.sessionId, transport);

  res.on("close", () => {
    sseTransports.delete(transport.sessionId);
  });

  // Connect McpServer with authenticated user context!
  const server = createTaskPulseServer({ authInfo: req.auth });
  await server.connect(transport);
});

// 6. SSE Message Receiver
app.post("/messages", async (req, res) => {
  const sessionId = req.query.sessionId as string;
  const transport = sseTransports.get(sessionId);

  if (!transport) {
    res.status(404).json({ error: "Session not found" });
    return;
  }

  await transport.handlePostMessage(req, res, req.body);
});

app.listen(PORT, () => {
  console.log(`🚀 TaskPulse MCP running at ${issuerUrl.href}`);
  console.log(`🔒 Protected SSE: ${issuerUrl.href}sse`);
  console.log(`📋 Metadata: ${issuerUrl.href}.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`);
});

Step 5: Implementing MCP Tools, Resources & Prompts with User Context

Now comes the fun part: writing the MCP functionality!

Because our authentication middleware attaches req.auth (AuthInfo), our server factory receives:

  • authInfo.extra.userId (Who is calling?)
  • authInfo.extra.orgId (Which workspace do they belong to?)
  • authInfo.scopes (What are they allowed to do?)

Create src/server.ts:

import { McpServer, ResourceTemplate } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js";
import { z } from "zod";
import type { AuthInfo } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/auth/types.js";

// Mock database
interface Task {
  id: string;
  orgId: string;
  title: string;
  status: "TODO" | "IN_PROGRESS" | "DONE";
  assigneeId: string;
}

const mockTasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "task_1", orgId: "org_engineering", title: "Write API documentation", status: "IN_PROGRESS", assigneeId: "usr_alex_101" },
  { id: "task_2", orgId: "org_engineering", title: "Set up CI/CD pipeline", status: "TODO", assigneeId: "usr_alex_101" },
];

export function createTaskPulseServer(options?: { authInfo?: AuthInfo }): McpServer {
  const server = new McpServer({
    name: "TaskPulse",
    version: "1.0.0",
  });

  const currentUser = options?.authInfo?.extra?.userId as string || "anonymous";
  const userOrg = options?.authInfo?.extra?.orgId as string || "default_org";
  const scopes = options?.authInfo?.scopes || [];

  // ==========================================
  // 1. TOOLS ("Do something")
  // ==========================================

  // TOOL: List Tasks (Scoped to user's organization)
  server.tool(
    "list_my_tasks",
    "List all tasks assigned to the current user in their organization.",
    {
      status: z.enum(["ALL", "TODO", "IN_PROGRESS", "DONE"]).default("ALL").optional(),
    },
    async (args) => {
      if (!scopes.includes("tasks:read")) {
        return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Forbidden: Missing 'tasks:read' scope" }], isError: true };
      }

      const tasks = mockTasks.filter(t => t.orgId === userOrg && t.assigneeId === currentUser);
      const filtered = args.status && args.status !== "ALL" ? tasks.filter(t => t.status === args.status) : tasks;

      return {
        content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(filtered, null, 2) }],
      };
    }
  );

  // TOOL: Create Task (Requires 'tasks:write' scope)
  server.tool(
    "create_task",
    "Create a new task in the current user's workspace.",
    {
      title: z.string().min(3).describe("Task title"),
      status: z.enum(["TODO", "IN_PROGRESS"]).default("TODO").optional(),
    },
    async (args) => {
      if (!scopes.includes("tasks:write")) {
        return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Forbidden: Missing 'tasks:write' scope" }], isError: true };
      }

      const newTask: Task = {
        id: `task_${Date.now()}`,
        orgId: userOrg,
        title: args.title,
        status: args.status || "TODO",
        assigneeId: currentUser,
      };
      mockTasks.push(newTask);

      return {
        content: [{
          type: "text",
          text: JSON.stringify({
            success: true,
            message: `Task created successfully by ${currentUser}`,
            task: newTask,
          }, null, 2)
        }],
      };
    }
  );

  // ==========================================
  // 2. RESOURCES ("Read context")
  // ==========================================

  // Dynamic Resource: Read project details
  server.resource(
    "project-details",
    new ResourceTemplate("taskpulse://projects/{projectId}", { list: undefined }),
    async (uri, { projectId }) => {
      const pid = Array.isArray(projectId) ? projectId[0] : projectId;
      return {
        contents: [{
          uri: uri.href,
          mimeType: "application/json",
          text: JSON.stringify({
            projectId: pid,
            organization: userOrg,
            lead: currentUser,
            description: "Core sprint engineering workspace.",
          }, null, 2),
        }],
      };
    }
  );

  // ==========================================
  // 3. PROMPTS ("Guide the conversation")
  // ==========================================

  // Prompt: Generate standup update based on tasks
  server.prompt(
    "sprint_standup_summary",
    "Generate a structured daily standup report for the current user's active tasks.",
    {
      includeBlockers: z.string().optional().describe("Ask if there are any blockers (yes/no)"),
    },
    (args) => ({
      messages: [{
        role: "user",
        content: {
          type: "text",
          text: `You are my agile project assistant. Look at my assigned tasks in TaskPulse for user ${currentUser} and write a concise 3-bullet standup summary:
1. What I completed yesterday
2. What I'm working on today
3. Blockers (${args.includeBlockers || "none declared"}).`,
        },
      }],
    })
  );

  return server;
}

11. Testing Your Server (Locally & in Claude/Cursor)

1. Run the Server 

# In your terminal
npm run build && node --max-http-header-size=65536 dist/index.js

2. Configure Claude Desktop

Open your configuration file:

  • macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
  • Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

Add your remote server:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "taskpulse": {
      "url": "http://localhost:8080/sse"
    }
  }
}

3. Watch the Magic Happen

  1. Start Claude Desktop.
  2. Claude hits http://localhost:8080/sse and receives the 401 Unauthorized with the Protected Resource header.
  3. Claude automatically opens your browser to: http://localhost:8080/authorize?client_id=claude-desktop&...
  4. You see your dark-mode TaskPulse consent screen!
  5. Enter alex@example.com and password correct-horse-battery, then click Authorize Access.
  6. The browser redirects to http://localhost/callback?code=....
  7. Claude exchanges the code for the JWT token and connects to the SSE stream.
  8. Ask Claude: > "What tasks are assigned to me in TaskPulse?" > Claude calls list_my_tasks and replies with your tasks! >

12. Production Gotchas & Best Practices

Here are four lessons we learned the hard way when deploying MCP servers:

1. Node.js Header Size Limit

  • The Issue: With OAuth JWTs, cookies, and CORS headers, requests can exceed Node's default header limit (8KB-16KB) and throw 431 Request Header Fields Too Large.
  • The Fix: Always start Node with --max-http-header-size=65536.

2. The Issuer URL in Cloud Deployments

  • The Issue: If your server issues tokens with iss: "http://localhost:8080", but your production server lives at https://mcp.yourdomain.com, token verification will fail.
  • The Fix: Dynamically set the issuerUrl using an environment variable (APP_URL): 
  const issuerUrl = new URL(process.env.APP_URL || `http://localhost:${PORT}`);

3. Store Tokens in Redis / Database in Production

  • In this tutorial, we used in-memory Maps for sessions and tokens.
  • In production, if your cloud provider restarts your container or runs multiple replicas, in-memory tokens will be lost. Store your authorization codes and refresh tokens in Redis or PostgreSQL.

4. Always Enforce Scope Verification Inside Tools

  • Don't just check if a user is logged in. Check what they are allowed to do! Check scopes.includes("tasks:write") before mutating data.

Happy building!

articles.title: WAMR3D: A Native WebAssembly 3D Engine with a three.js-Style API and Its Own WebGPU Renderer
articles.description: WAMR3D is a Rust and WebAssembly 3D engine with its own WebGPU renderer and a three.js-style API. Change one import, and batch your hot paths for up to about 8x less draw-submission CPU time than three.js WebGPU.
articles.body_html:
If you have ever shipped a three.js scene with thousands of animated objects, you know where the frame budget goes: JavaScript object updates, matrix math, and the cost of handing draw calls to the GPU. WAMR3D is a new open-source attempt at that problem. It moves the scene graph, transforms, culling, and draw ordering into a Rust core compiled to WebAssembly, pairs it with a WebGPU renderer written from scratch, and keeps an API that reads like three.js.

Here is what it is, what it measures, and where it still falls short.

  • Website: wamr3d.org
  • npm: wamr3d
  • GitHub: aymen94/wamr3d

What is WAMR3D?

WAMR3D is a WebAssembly 3D rendering engine with a Rust core and a separate WebGPU renderer. It is not a wrapper around three.js. It is also not a finished replacement for it. The project is young, and the README says so directly.

Three parts make it up:

  1. A native core in WebAssembly. The scene graph, world matrices, frustum culling, draw ordering, and raycasting run inside a Wasm module.
  2. Its own WebGPU renderer. Meshes, lines, points, sprites, and instanced meshes. Basic, Lambert, and standard materials. Colour textures, fog, up to 16 lights, PCF shadows, tone mapping, render targets, and 4× MSAA.
  3. A three.js-style object API under wamr3d/compat, plus a lower-level batched API for large scenes.

The license is MIT. There are no runtime dependencies, and the Wasm module is about 488 KiB.

Why a native core matters for three.js developers

In most three.js apps, scene state lives in JavaScript objects. Every position.set(), rotation.y +=, and matrix update is JavaScript work, and the garbage collector eventually gets involved.

WAMR3D takes a different approach:

  • The scene lives in engine memory. Objects are created and destroyed explicitly in WebAssembly, so the engine itself adds no GC pauses.
  • Generational handles. A handle to a destroyed object can never silently point at a different object.
  • Zero-copy geometry. You can read and write vertex attributes through typed-array views directly over engine memory.
  • Batched sync. In the object API, position, rotation, and scale stay in JavaScript, and every change is sent to the engine in a single batch per frame.

The result is that WAMR3D wins when you batch work, and loses when you make many tiny calls. The project documents both.

Measured performance

These are the numbers from the repo's benchmark record, recorded on 2026-10-14 in headless Chrome on Windows x64 with an RTX 2070 SUPER. They are medians from a single run per resolution on one machine. Treat them as a starting point, and measure your own scene.

10,000 separate animated meshes at 1920×1080:

Engine fps Draw submission (CPU)
WAMR3D, batched API 60.0 12.2 ms
WAMR3D, object API 60.0 12.3 ms
three.js WebGPU 9.5 100.5 ms
three.js WebGL 33.7 23.7 ms

50,000 instanced bodies, scene update on the CPU: 12.0 ms for WAMR3D's batched API, against 39.1 ms for three.js WebGPU and 39.7 ms for three.js WebGL.

Put simply: in this showcase, WAMR3D spends roughly 8× less CPU time on draw submission than three.js WebGPU, and about 1.9× less than three.js WebGL. The frame rate caps at 60 because the showcase has a display limit.

The project also publishes the other side of the picture. Calls that do very little work, such as a single vector operation or one property at a time, measured 1.3× to 3.8× slower than three.js, because crossing into WebAssembly has a fixed cost. GPU time is not measured separately; it only shows up in the frame rate.

If you want to check these yourself, the showcase page runs all four renderers live: wamr3d.org/examples/showcase.

Same results as three.js, checked by tests

Speed means nothing if the output is wrong. WAMR3D replays over 7,600 reference cases generated from the three.js r186 source against the Rust code. Individual operations agree to about one part in a million. All 23 renderer test cases are compared pixel by pixel against stored three.js images.

The repo also includes 643 Rust tests covering unit, parity, and allocation behaviour, plus a visual parity page that shows each WAMR3D render next to the three.js image and the pixel difference.

Get started in two minutes 

npm install wamr3d

Change the import, initialize once, and switch to the WebGPU renderer:

- import * as THREE from 'three';
+ import * as THREE from 'wamr3d/compat';
+ await THREE.init();

- const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer( { antialias: true } );
+ const renderer = new THREE.WebGPURenderer( { antialias: true } );
+ await renderer.init();

A complete example:

import * as WAMR3D from 'wamr3d/compat';

await WAMR3D.init();

const scene = new WAMR3D.Scene();
const camera = new WAMR3D.PerspectiveCamera(50, innerWidth / innerHeight, 0.1, 100);
camera.position.set(3, 2, 5);
camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);

const cube = new WAMR3D.Mesh(
  new WAMR3D.BoxGeometry(),
  new WAMR3D.MeshLambertMaterial({ color: 0x4f8cff })
);
scene.add(cube, new WAMR3D.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 2));

const renderer = new WAMR3D.WebGPURenderer({ antialias: true });
await renderer.init();
renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  cube.rotation.y = time / 1000;
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
});

scene.add, position.set, rotation.y +=, lookAt, and raycasting work as written for the classes WAMR3D supports. The project's migration guide lists exactly which classes exist and what to watch for.

Requirements: a browser with WebGPU (current Chrome or Edge), served over HTTP rather than file://. Node.js 18 or newer can run the math and scene graph without a renderer.

Batching for large scenes

When your scene grows past a few hundred objects, the batched API is where the gains come from. Handles and calls like setRotations update thousands of objects in one crossing into WebAssembly. You read world matrices through typed-array views without copying them.

The low-level API is also exported directly from wamr3d:

import { init, World } from 'wamr3d';

await init();

const world = new World();
const scene = world.createObject();
const arm = world.createObject();
const hand = world.createObject();
world.add(scene, arm);
world.add(arm, hand);

world.setPosition(arm, 10, 0, 0);
world.setRotation(arm, 0, 0, Math.PI / 2, 'XYZ');
world.setPosition(hand, 1, 0, 0);

world.updateMatrixWorld(scene, false);
console.log(world.matrixWorld(hand)); // Float32Array(16), column-major

Two details to know: matrices are column-major, and the low-level API has no default arguments, so rotation order and similar parameters are always written out.

What is not there yet

This section matters most, so here it is in full. From the project's own status page, the following are not available yet:

  • Environment reflections (not connected to scene.environment or envMap)
  • Point-light shadows and area lights
  • Post-processing and scene background textures
  • Most loaders, animation, audio, and controls (the exception is TextureLoader)
  • Shadow modes other than PCF
  • A WebGL fallback

It has also been verified only in Node.js v24 and headless Chrome. Firefox, Safari, and bundler setups have not been tried yet.

For those features, keep three.js for now.

Who this is for

WAMR3D is a good fit if you:

  • Have a three.js scene with many objects, and the bottleneck is JavaScript updates or draw submission
  • Are experimenting with WebGPU and want a renderer that is not a thin wrapper
  • Care about deterministic, checked behaviour, and want to see the parity tests
  • Want to contribute to a Rust and WebAssembly graphics engine

It is probably not the right choice yet if you depend on post-processing, environment maps, loaders, animation, or Firefox and Safari support.

Try it, measure it, tell me what breaks

The fastest way to judge WAMR3D is to run it on your own scene:

  • Live demos: WebGPU renderer, showcase, side-by-side comparison
  • Migration guide: MIGRATION.md
  • Status and benchmarks: STATUS.md
  • Design decisions: DECISIONS.md

The project has one star and no forks so far, so early feedback will shape it a lot. Issues, benchmark results from other GPUs, and reports from Firefox or Safari are all useful. If you find a case where it is slower than three.js, please open an issue. The project explicitly values those results.

Star it on GitHub, and try npm install wamr3d on a scene you already know.

WAMR3D is an independent project, not affiliated with three.js. It is inspired by three.js and credits it throughout the repository.

articles.title: Stripping EXIF and GPS from photos in the browser, losslessly, in ~500 lines of vanilla JS
articles.description: Photos from phones carry more than pixels. Open the file and there's often the exact GPS position it...
articles.body_html:
Photos from phones carry more than pixels. Open the file and there's often the exact GPS position it was taken at, the phone model, lens and settings, the date and time, sometimes the owner's name or a camera serial number, and, increasingly, labels saying whether an image was edited with generative AI.

I make a small Android camera app, and people kept asking whether the photos they share give away where they live. So I built a checker that shows what a photo file carries and saves a clean copy, without uploading anything:

https://blinqdroid.com/tools/photo-privacy-check/

No libraries, no server, no WebAssembly: a DataView over the file's bytes. Here's how it works.

Reading the file without uploading it

The whole thing starts with the bytes in memory:

const u8 = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());

From there it's container walking. The first bytes tell you the format: FF D8 is a JPEG, 89 PNG is a PNG, RIFF....WEBP is a WebP, and II/MM at the start is a TIFF (which is also what a DNG raw file is).

JPEG: walking the markers

A JPEG is a list of segments. Each starts with 0xFF, a marker byte, then a two-byte big-endian length:

let p = 2; // skip SOI (FF D8)
while (p + 4 <= u8.length) {
  if (u8[p] !== 0xFF) { p++; continue; }
  const m = u8[p + 1];
  const len = (u8[p + 2] << 8) | u8[p + 3];
  const start = p + 4, n = len - 2;
  if (m === 0xE1 && ascii(u8, start, 6) === 'Exif\0\0') readTiff(u8, start + 6, n - 6);
  // APP1 can also hold XMP: "http://ns.adobe.com/xap/1.0/\0" + XML
  p = start + n;
}

The fiddly part is the image data itself. After a Start of Scan (FF DA) segment comes entropy-coded data with no length field. Inside it, a literal 0xFF byte is "stuffed" as FF 00, and restart markers FF D0–FF D7 can appear. So to find the next real segment (progressive JPEGs have several scans, with tables in between) you scan forward for an 0xFF that is followed by something other than 00 or a restart marker.

EXIF is a tiny TIFF file

The EXIF block is a TIFF structure: a byte-order mark (II little-endian, MM big-endian), the number 42, and an offset to the first IFD (image file directory). Each IFD entry is 12 bytes: tag, type, count, and either the value or an offset to it.

const le = ascii(u8, base, 2) === 'II';
const dv = new DataView(u8.buffer, u8.byteOffset + base);
const count = dv.getUint16(ifdOffset, le);
for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
  const e = ifdOffset + 2 + i * 12;
  const tag = dv.getUint16(e, le), type = dv.getUint16(e + 2, le);
  // 0x8769 points to the Exif sub-IFD, 0x8825 to the GPS IFD
}

GPS coordinates are three rationals (degrees, minutes, seconds), each a pair of 32-bit integers, plus a reference letter:

const dms = ([d, m, s], ref) => (d + m / 60 + s / 3600) * (/[SW]/.test(ref) ? -1 : 1);

The IFD after the first one (IFD1) is the embedded thumbnail. It's easy to forget, and it can still show the uncropped original after you've cropped the photo.

PNG, WebP and the AI labels

PNG is a list of chunks (length, type, data, CRC). Metadata lives in eXIf (the same TIFF structure), tEXt/iTXt/zTXt text chunks and tIME. Some image generators write their whole prompt into a tEXt chunk called parameters, so the tool shows text chunks verbatim.

WebP is RIFF: four-character chunk IDs with little-endian sizes, padded to even lengths. EXIF and XMP are separate chunks, and the VP8X header has flag bits saying they're present.

In XMP, the interesting fields for 2026 are the IPTC DigitalSourceType values (trainedAlgorithmicMedia means made with generative AI, compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia edited with it) and whether a Content Credentials (C2PA) manifest is embedded. The tool only detects C2PA; it doesn't validate the signature.

Cleaning without re-compressing

The easy way to strip metadata is to draw the image on a canvas and export it. That re-encodes the JPEG and loses quality. Instead, for JPEG, PNG and WebP the tool rebuilds the file from the parts it keeps:

  • JPEG: keep everything except APP1–APP15 and COM segments, with two exceptions: the ICC colour profile (APP2 "ICC_PROFILE") and Adobe's APP14, because dropping those changes how colours display. The image data is copied byte for byte.
  • PNG: drop eXIf, tEXt, iTXt, zTXt, tIME and the C2PA caBX chunk.
  • WebP: drop EXIF and XMP chunks, clear their bits in VP8X, and rewrite the RIFF size.

One catch with JPEGs: phones often store the image sideways and add an Orientation tag saying how to display it. Strip all EXIF and the photo shows up rotated. So the clean JPEG gets a brand-new 36-byte EXIF segment containing exactly one tag, Orientation, and nothing else.

Other formats the browser can decode (AVIF, for example) fall back to a canvas re-encode as JPEG at quality 0.95. DNG is read-only, and HEIC can only be cleaned in browsers that can decode it.

Proving it worked

Before offering the download, the page runs the same parser on the clean copy and reports anything left. It's a small step, but it turns "trust me" into "here's what the output contains":

const again = summary(analyse(new Uint8Array(await blob.arrayBuffer())));
const left = ['location', 'identity', 'device', 'time', 'software', 'ai'].filter(k => again[k].length);

Privacy, verifiably

The page runs under a strict Content Security Policy (no inline scripts, no third-party scripts), and the photo never leaves the tab: load the page, switch off your network, and it still works. The script isn't minified, so you can read it at /js/photo-check.js. The only request it makes is to my own page counter, saying that a photo was checked or cleaned. There are no cookies and no photo data in it.

If you find a file it misreads, I'd love to hear about it in the comments: the metadata, not the photo, or a test file with fake details.

articles.title: Why I made GalionToon process everything in the browser (and never upload your files)
articles.description: Why I made GalionToon process everything in the browser (and never upload your files)  I still...
articles.body_html:
Why I made GalionToon process everything in the browser (and never upload your files)

I still remember the moment I decided this project had to exist.

A friend sent me a PSD file to review. Nothing sensitive, just a design draft. I opened my usual tools, made a couple of adjustments, and then stopped mid-click.

Where did that file just go?

I knew the answer. It went to a server. Somewhere. Owned by someone. Stored for an amount of time I couldn't verify. Processed by systems I couldn't audit.

That bothered me more than it should have. Not because anything bad happened — it didn't. But because I realized I had been trusting silently for years.

Every time I edited a photo, opened a PSD, generated a sprite sheet, or cleaned up a video subtitle, I was sending my work somewhere else.

So I built GalionToon.

🎨 What GalionToon is

GalionToon is a free creative suite that runs entirely in your browser. It has five independent studios:

Studio What it does
🖼️ Galion Photo Photo and PSD editing
🦌 Galion Rig 2D animation with bones
🎮 Pixel Galion Pixel art editor
🎬 Video Editor Video cutting and subtitles
📻 Radio Galion Music while you work

No installs. No accounts. No uploads. Everything you do stays on your machine.

👉 You can try it at galiontoon.com.

☁️ The problem with "the cloud"

I'm not against servers. I use cloud services every day.

But I started noticing a pattern in creative software:

  • ❌ Files get uploaded "for processing"
  • ❌ Projects live on remote storage
  • ❌ Features get locked behind subscriptions
  • ❌ Privacy policies are pages long and written in a language no one reads

For a professional workflow, this is fine. You trust your employer's IT team to vet the tools.

But for everyone else — hobbyists, students, indie artists, game developers working from home — it's a quiet trade-off they never agreed to.

I wanted to offer an alternative. Not a superior one. Just a different one.

One where the default is: your files never leave your device.

⚙️ How it actually works

Processing everything in the browser is harder than it sounds. Here's what I learned building GalionToon.

1️⃣ Modern browsers are incredibly powerful

Ten years ago, this project would have been impossible. Today, the browser gives you:

  • 🎨 Canvas API and WebGL for rendering
  • ⚡ WebAssembly for near-native performance
  • 📁 File System Access API for opening and saving files locally
  • 🎬 WebCodecs API for video decoding without uploading
  • 🔌 Service Workers for offline functionality

Everything GalionToon does is possible because the web platform matured. I just had to use it.

2️⃣ PSD parsing in pure JavaScript

One of the biggest technical challenges was PSD support. Adobe's format is complex:

  • Layers
  • Groups
  • Masks
  • Blend modes
  • Editable text
  • Effects

I wrote a parser that reads the PSD structure directly in the browser. It handles the common cases and gracefully degrades on advanced features.

The file never leaves the user's computer. Not even for a millisecond.

3️⃣ Performance without a server

The hardest problem was performance on large canvases.

When you edit a 4K PSD with 50 layers, you can't just redraw everything on every brush stroke.

The solution is spatial caching: only redraw the area that actually changed.

Combined with offscreen canvases and WebGL acceleration, this gets us to 60 FPS on mid-range hardware.

I spent weeks on this. It's the kind of optimization you don't notice when it works — you only notice it when it doesn't.

4️⃣ Animation with bones

Galion Rig uses inverse kinematics to animate 2D characters.

The math is straightforward (for small chains), but the interaction design is where things get interesting:

  • You drag the tip of a bone → the whole chain adjusts
  • You paint influence weights
  • You set keyframes

None of this requires a server. It's just math and canvas rendering.

5️⃣ Video subtitles without uploading

The video editor generates subtitles locally.

This was the most surprising win: modern models can run in the browser via WebAssembly or ONNX Runtime. They download once, cache locally, and work offline.

Your footage never leaves your device.

💚 What this means for users

When I talk to artists and developers who've tried GalionToon, the reaction is always the same: relief.

Not because it's revolutionary. But because it removes a layer of anxiety they didn't know they had.

  • ✅ You can open a client's PSD without uploading it to a random server
  • ✅ You can edit sensitive photos without them being processed by a third party
  • ✅ You can work on a plane, offline, without losing functionality
  • ✅ You can use it on a Chromebook, a locked-down work laptop, or a friend's computer

Privacy isn't a feature. It's a default.

🧠 What I got wrong along the way

I want to be honest about the project's limitations.

⚠️ Performance is harder than expected.
Chromium's GPU handling can degrade silently. I've spent more hours than I want to admit chasing performance bugs on older hardware.

⚠️ Compatibility is incomplete.
PSD is a moving target. Some features work perfectly, others partially, others not at all. I document everything in COMPATIBILITY.txt.

⚠️ Importing assets is tricky.
Brush formats like .abr or .kpp are proprietary. I support the basics but not everything.

⚠️ Translations take time.
Right now GalionToon is available in Spanish, English, and French. More languages are planned, but each one is a serious investment.

None of these are dealbreakers. They're just the reality of building something ambitious alone.

💡 Why I'm sharing this

DEV Community has taught me a lot over the years. So I want to give back something useful: a real example of what's possible when you take browser capabilities seriously.

If you're building something and wondering whether to keep it client-side or move it to a server, here's my honest take:

Keep it client-side as long as you can.

The moment you add a server, you inherit:

  • 💸 Infrastructure costs
  • 🔒 Privacy obligations
  • 🔧 Maintenance burden
  • ⚖️ Legal complexity
  • 🚨 A permanent risk surface

For many projects, this is fine. For a creative tool where users upload personal work, it's an unnecessary trade-off.

🚀 Try it and tell me what you think

GalionToon is free and available now:

  • 🌐 galiontoon.com
  • 📦 itch.io page

If you build something with it, I'd love to see it.
If you find a bug, tell me.
If you have an idea for a feature that would make it more useful, I'm listening.

And if you're working on something similar — a browser-based tool that respects privacy — reach out. I'd love to compare notes.

📝 Thanks for reading. This is the first of a series I'm writing about building GalionToon. Next: how I got PSD parsing to work in pure JavaScript, and what I learned about the format in the process.

articles.title: Why collapsible tab headers jump in React Native (and how to fix it)
articles.description: You've seen this screen a hundred times: a profile header, a row of tabs underneath (Posts, Media,...
articles.body_html:
You've seen this screen a hundred times: a profile header, a row of tabs underneath (Posts, Media, Likes), and the header collapses as you scroll. Twitter, Instagram, Spotify artist pages.

Now try this on most implementations:

  1. Scroll Posts down a few screens. The header collapses.
  2. Switch to Media, which is still at the top.
  3. Watch the header jump: snap open, snap closed, or leave a gap.

I hit this enough times that I ended up writing my own library. Here's what's actually going on.

The root cause: the header is derived from the active tab's scroll

The common approach is simple: headerTranslateY = -clamp(activeTab.scrollY, 0, headerHeight).

It works perfectly with one tab. With several, every tab has its own scroll offset, and the header position is a function of whichever tab is active. Switch tabs and the input changes instantly, so the output (your header) teleports.

Libraries usually patch around it by force-syncing scroll offsets on every tab switch (scrolling the new tab to match the header). That's where you get flicker, lost scroll positions, and fights with list virtualization.

The fix: decouple the header from tab offsets

Instead of deriving the header from a scroll offset, make the header position its own piece of state (a Reanimated shared value), and drive it with scroll deltas:

  • Scrolling down collapses the header in sync with content.
  • Scrolling up keeps the header collapsed until the content's top edge reaches it, then expands it in sync. The header never detaches from content and never leaves a gap.
  • Switching tabs doesn't touch the header at all. Each tab keeps its own scroll position, and the header stays exactly where it was.

No offset-syncing, no jump, and every tab remembers where you left it.

The trade-off (there's always one)

Because each tab keeps its own scroll memory, a deep-scrolled tab can have content sitting underneath an expanded header. So the header needs a solid background; translucent headers don't work with this model. I think that's the right trade for jump-free switching, but it's worth knowing upfront.

In practice

▶️ Watch the demo: switching tabs with zero header jump

I packaged this approach as react-native-collapsible-tab. It's built on Reanimated, Gesture Handler and Pager View, with all animation on the UI thread.

npm install react-native-collapsible-tab
npx expo install react-native-reanimated react-native-gesture-handler react-native-pager-view

import { Tabs } from 'react-native-collapsible-tab';

function Profile() {
  return (
    <Tabs.Container
      renderHeader={() => <ProfileHeader />} // height measured automatically
      minHeaderHeight={insets.top}           // stays visible when collapsed
      lazy                                   // mount tabs on first focus
      snapThreshold={0.5}                    // settle fully open/closed on release
    >
      <Tabs.Tab name="posts" label="Posts">
        <Tabs.FlatList
          data={posts}
          renderItem={({ item }) => <Post post={item} />}
          keyExtractor={(item) => item.id}
        />
      </Tabs.Tab>
      <Tabs.Tab name="media" label="Media">
        <Tabs.ScrollView>
          <MediaGrid />
        </Tabs.ScrollView>
      </Tabs.Tab>
    </Tabs.Container>
  );
}

A few things I cared about while building it:

  • Twitter-style reveal: revealHeaderOnScroll brings the header back on any upward scroll.
  • Snap without deadlocks: snap is a plain shared-value animation, not offset-driven scrolling, which is known to lock up the UI thread on the New Architecture.
  • FlashList v2 and LegendList adapters, plus FlatList, ScrollView and SectionList.
  • Windowed memory: with React 19.2's <Activity>, windowConfig={{ ahead: 1, behind: 1 }} keeps 60 tabs from all staying mounted. Only the focused one and its neighbours stay live, and scroll positions survive.

One gotcha that bites everyone: negative scroll offsets

If you animate anything from scroll position (a progress bar, a fade), remember that on iOS contentOffset.y goes negative when the list bounces past the top. Android clamps at 0. Clamp both ends:

// ❌ negative offset → negative width during bounce
width: `${Math.min((scrollY.value / TOTAL) * 100, 100)}%`

// ✅ overscroll reads as 0%
width: `${Math.max(0, Math.min((scrollY.value / TOTAL) * 100, 100))}%`

bounces={false} hides the symptom; clamping is the actual fix.

Docs: rnct.scannertechs.com · GitHub: JassiSingh08/react-native-collapsible-tab

If you've fought this bug with a different approach, I'd love to hear how you solved it in the comments.

articles.title: I Ship 61 Calculators as a Static Site in 12 Languages — Here's How
articles.description: I Ship 61 Calculators as a Static Site in 12 Languages — Here's How   We're a small team of...
articles.body_html:
I Ship 61 Calculators as a Static Site in 12 Languages — Here's How

We're a small team of software engineers, and we run youcancalc.com — a free collection of 61 calculators, localized into 12 languages. No accounts, no backend, no paywall, no tracking pixels. Every calculation happens in your browser. This is a notes-from-the-trenches post about the architecture choices that make that possible, and the ones we'd make again.

The whole thing is static

The site is a statically-exported site: every page is pre-rendered to plain HTML at build time and served as files. There is no application server, no database, no API to keep warm. A calculator page is a document with a script attached, not an app with a backend.

This sounds limiting until you realize what a calculator actually needs: inputs, arithmetic, and formatted output. None of that requires a server round-trip. The result is pages that answer instantly — no spinners, no "computing..." states — and hosting that is boring in the best way.

All computation is client-side

Each calculator page follows the same contract:

  1. Inputs — the user types numbers, picks options.
  2. Instant result — recomputed on every keystroke, locally.
  3. How it works — the formula is printed next to the answer, not hidden.
  4. Worked examples — concrete numbers walked through step by step.
  5. FAQ — the questions people actually ask about this calculation.
  6. Related calculators — the natural next questions.

Because everything runs client-side, there's a privacy property we get for free and take seriously: your inputs never leave your browser. There's nothing to leak because there's nowhere for the data to go. We don't have your numbers; we never did. In an era where every form field seems to phone home, "the architecture makes surveillance impossible" is a stronger guarantee than any privacy policy paragraph.

i18n without a translation department

Twelve locales: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Arabic, Dutch, Polish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean. A few things we learned doing this as a tiny team:

Locale-prefixed routes. Every language lives under its own path prefix (/es/, /de/, …), so each locale is a fully crawlable, shareable site — not a JavaScript-swapped afterthought.

Localize everything, including the math. Formulas, worked examples, and FAQs are content, not chrome — they all go through the i18n layer. A French user should read the explanation of compound interest in French, not just the buttons.

Numbers are not universal. This is the bug class that keeps us humble. Intl.NumberFormat exists for a reason: 1,234.56 in English is 1.234,56 in German. Decimal separators, digit grouping, and even digit shapes differ. Every numeric input and output goes through locale-aware formatting and parsing — parse with the locale, never with parseFloat on raw user input.

RTL is a layout commitment. Arabic means right-to-left, and that affects more than text direction: form layouts, example tables, and the visual order of "inputs → result" all need to mirror correctly. We test it; it's the kind of thing that's either right or embarrassing.

What we deliberately don't do

Constraints are features. We don't do accounts (nothing to personalize), we don't do paywalls (the calculators are the product, and they're free), and we don't do tracking (see above: nothing to track with). We also don't have a blog — each calculator page carries its own explanation, examples, and FAQ, so the content lives where the question is asked instead of in a separate content silo.

This keeps the operational surface tiny: no user data to protect, no sessions to manage, no email infrastructure, no A/B testing apparatus watching your mouse. The site is, by construction, a very boring thing to operate. We like boring.

The honest trade-offs

Static has costs and we won't pretend otherwise:

  • Build time grows with locales × pages. 61 calculators × 12 languages is hundreds of pages per build. It's fine on modern hardware, but it's the thing we watch.
  • No personalization. We can't remember your last calculation across devices, because we don't know who you are. We consider this acceptable — arguably it's the point.
  • Client-side means client constraints. Very old browsers and very slow devices get a degraded but functional experience; we keep the client-side script lean and avoid heavy client libraries rather than assuming a flagship phone.
  • Translation quality is an ongoing process. Machine-assisted translation gets you 90% of the way; the last 10% — idioms in FAQs, culturally specific examples — needs human eyes, and with 12 locales it's never "done."

Why this architecture fits calculators specifically

A calculator is a pure function with a nice UI: same inputs, same outputs, every time. There's no shared state, no feed, no real-time collaboration. The moment you notice your product is embarrassingly parallel and stateless, the correct architecture is usually "files on a CDN." We just took that seriously and stopped there instead of adding a backend out of habit.

If you're building something similar — reference tools, converters, small utilities — our sincere recommendation: start static, compute locally, and only add a server when you can name the specific thing it does that the browser can't. You might be surprised how rarely that day comes.

We're the team behind youcancalc — 61 free calculators, 12 languages, zero tracking. If you build tiny tools on the web, we'd genuinely like to hear how you architect them.

articles.title: Keeping declarativeNetRequest rules in sync after a Manifest V3 service worker restarts
articles.description: By mid-afternoon, my Chrome usually had 40+ tabs open across three windows. I tried several tab...
articles.body_html:
By mid-afternoon, my Chrome usually had 40+ tabs open across three windows. I tried several tab managers, but they either demanded a cloud account, locked basic features behind a subscription, or only solved one half of the problem.

So I spent the last few months building my own: PYLON, an offline-first New Tab that pairs project tab workspaces with dev tools and a deep-focus Pomodoro timer.

This post is about one specific engineering challenge: the site blocker.

The hardest part wasn’t intercepting requests — it was deciding what the source of truth should be when a Manifest V3 background service worker constantly terminates and restarts.

The setup

When a focus session starts, the extension redirects configured distraction sites to a local focus-intercept.html page bundled inside the extension.

I chose Chrome's modern declarativeNetRequest (DNR) API over old blocking webRequests so that the browser itself evaluates rules at native speed without injecting custom JavaScript into the request path.

Three pieces of state have to stay consistent:

What Where it lives Why
Blocked domains chrome.storage.local Survives restarts, handles crashes, easily exported
Active redirect rules DNR Dynamic Rules Evaluated directly by the browser network stack
Rule IDs A reserved ID range (1000–1999) Ensures we only delete focus rules without touching other extension rules

My core rule: chrome.storage.local is the sole source of truth. DNR rules are merely a temporary mirror of it.

Step 1: Clean and normalize user input

Users paste whatever happens to be in their address bar:

  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=...
  • reddit.com/r/webdev
  • x.com:443

Because DNR rules match against hostname patterns (typically using ||domain.com^), passing raw URLs will break rule matching. Every entry must be cleaned to a bare domain before touching storage:

const cleaned = Array.from(new Set((domains || [])
  .map(d => String(d || '').trim().toLowerCase()
    .replace(/^https?:\/\//, '')   // drop the protocol
    .replace(/\/.*$/, '')          // drop any trailing path
    .split(':')[0].split('?')[0])  // drop port numbers and query parameters
  .filter(Boolean)));

Step 2: Rebuild the rules — don't patch them

My initial instinct was incremental updates: add a rule when a user adds a domain, remove one when deleted.

In Manifest V3, incremental patching is an anti-pattern.

Service workers can terminate at any point of idle time. If an event wakes the worker while a write is resolving, or if two storage events trigger simultaneously, incremental updates can leave stale, orphaned rule IDs in the browser engine.

Instead, I adopted an idempotent reconciliation pattern:

  1. Read existing dynamic rules.
  2. Filter for rule IDs belonging to my reserved range.
  3. In a single atomic updateDynamicRules() call, delete all stale IDs and re-apply fresh rules generated from storage.
  4. Retry with backoff if Chrome's internal database locks. 
async function reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount = 0) {
  try {
    const existing = await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.getDynamicRules();
    const staleIds = existing
      .map(r => r.id)
      .filter(id => id >= FOCUS_RULE_ID_START && id <= FOCUS_RULE_ID_END);

    await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.updateDynamicRules({
      removeRuleIds: staleIds,
      addRules: buildShieldRules(expectedDomains || [])
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (retryCount < 3) {
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500));
      await reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount + 1);
    }
  }
}

If the focus session ends, passing an empty array automatically clears all rules in that range.

Step 3: Sweeping already-open tabs

One gotcha with declarativeNetRequest: redirect rules only apply to new network requests.

If a user already has YouTube open in a tab and starts a focus sprint, that tab remains accessible until they click a link or refresh.

To make the block instant, the activation sequence performs a quick tab sweep right after reconciling DNR rules:

const tabs = await chrome.tabs.query({});
for (const tab of tabs) {
  if (tab.url && isDomainBlocked(tab.url, expectedDomains)) {
    chrome.tabs.update(tab.id, { 
      url: chrome.runtime.getURL('focus-intercept.html') 
    });
  }
}

Questions for other extension developers:

Building on Manifest V3 has been an interesting exercise in distributed-systems thinking inside a single browser:

  1. Retry Strategy: Is a static 500ms delay sufficient for DNR rule updates, or have you found exponential backoff necessary under heavy browser load?
  2. Reconciliation Frequency: Do you reconcile DNR rules on every service worker startup (chrome.runtime.onStartup), or strictly when storage change listeners fire?
  3. Race Condition Testing: Has anyone established a reliable local testing setup for simulating abrupt service worker termination during active DNR writes?

If you've tackled DNR sync differently, I’d love to hear your approach in the comments.

Try it out:

If you're looking for an offline-first tab manager with native Chrome Tab Groups sync, developer tools (CORS toggle, localhost port monitor), and this focus shield:

👉 PYLON on the Chrome Web Store (Free, 100% offline, zero accounts/tracking)

articles.title: Your .env hit git. Here's how I keep secrets on a VPS
articles.description: I pushed a small Node + Postgres Compose stack to a private repo and only then noticed .env was in...
articles.body_html:
I pushed a small Node + Postgres Compose stack to a private repo and only then noticed .env was in the first commit. DATABASE_URL had a real password. Adding .gitignore afterward did nothing useful: Git still had the blob, and git check-ignore stayed quiet while the path was tracked.

This is the layout I use on a VPS now. Everything below was run on the box on 2026-10-15 with git 2.47.3, Docker Engine 26.1.5, Compose 2.26.1 and Node 20. Numbers and command output are from those runs.

TL;DR

  • Put .env in .gitignore before the first commit. Commit .env.example with fake values. If .env already landed in git, git rm --cached only stops future commits. The old blob stays until you rewrite history or rotate the secret.
  • On the VPS, keep real secrets in a file mode 600 (for example secrets.env) and point Compose at it with env_file. Do not put ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} in the YAML if that value comes from a project .env you might commit.
  • Compose interpolates ${...} in the Compose file itself, including inside command: strings. A JS template literal like `token=${t}` becomes empty before the container starts. Prefer a script file, or write $$t.

What are you actually protecting?

Three different places can hold the same password. Fixing one does not fix the others.

Place What goes wrong What fixes it
Git history Clone, fork, or a future public flip exposes the blob forever Never commit it; if you did, rotate and treat history as burned
File on the VPS Any local account can read a 644 secrets file chmod 600, owner = the deploy user
Process environment docker compose config, crash dumps, child processes Prefer env_file; avoid baking secrets into resolved YAML via ${}

.gitignore only affects the first column, and only for paths that are not already tracked.

How does .env end up in git?

I reproduced the failure in a throwaway repo. First commit included .env. Then I added:

.env
.env.*
!.env.example

After that commit, Git still listed .env:

$ git check-ignore -v .env
# (no output: still tracked, so ignore rules do not apply)

$ git ls-files | grep env
.env
.env.example

$ git show "$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD):.env" | head -3
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:[REDACTED]@db:5432/app
EPURE_DSN=https://[REDACTED]@ingest.example.com/1
NODE_ENV=production

git rm --cached .env plus a new commit makes check-ignore work again:

$ git rm --cached .env
$ git commit -m "stop tracking .env (too late for history)"
$ git check-ignore -v .env
.gitignore:1:.env   .env

The first commit still has the file. git rev-list --objects --all still showed the .env blob. Ignore files are not a time machine.

The correct order is boring and it works. Create .gitignore and .env.example first, then add:

$ git status --short
A  .env.example
A  .gitignore
A  app.js
# .env is absent from the index

$ git check-ignore -v .env
.gitignore:1:.env   .env

$ git ls-files
.env.example
.gitignore
app.js

No secret string in git grep across $(git rev-list --all).

What goes on the VPS?

I keep two files next to the Compose project:

  • .env.example in git: keys and fake values, so a teammate knows what to create.
  • secrets.env on the host only: real values, mode 600, listed in .gitignore. 
$ chmod 600 secrets.env
$ stat -c '%a %n' secrets.env .env.worldreadable
600 secrets.env
644 .env.worldreadable

On the lab box, Python reported other_read=False for 600 and other_read=True for 644. Same owner can read both. Every other account on the VPS can read the 644 copy.

A minimal systemd unit can load the same file:

[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/opt/app
EnvironmentFile=/etc/app/secrets.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /opt/app/server.js

Same rule: /etc/app/secrets.env is 600, not in git.

Compose: env_file vs ${PASSWORD} in the YAML

Compose loads a project .env for interpolation in the Compose file. That is separate from what the container sees as process.env.

Bad shape (host .env supplies ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}, and the resolved config prints it):

# compose.bad.yml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16.15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: app
  app:
    image: node:22.23.3-alpine
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/app
      APP_SECRET: ${APP_SECRET}

$ docker compose -f compose.bad.yml config | grep -E 'PASSWORD|DATABASE_URL|APP_SECRET'
      APP_SECRET: from-host-dotenv
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:HostInterpolatedSecret@db:5432/app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: HostInterpolatedSecret

That was 2 plaintext hits for HostInterpolatedSecret in the full config dump. Fine for local debugging. Bad to paste into an issue, a CI log, or a screenshot.

Better shape: put secrets in secrets.env, mount them with env_file, and keep the YAML free of ${SECRET}:

# compose.yml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16.15-alpine
    env_file:
      - secrets.env
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_DB: app
      # POSTGRES_PASSWORD comes from secrets.env

  app:
    image: node:22.23.3-alpine
    working_dir: /app
    volumes:
      - ./print-env.js:/app/print-env.js:ro
    env_file:
      - secrets.env
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_HOST: db
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    command: ["node", "print-env.js"]

// print-env.js
const u = process.env.POSTGRES_USER;
const p = process.env.POSTGRES_PASSWORD;
const h = process.env.POSTGRES_HOST;
const d = process.env.POSTGRES_DB;
console.log("password_in_process_env", Boolean(p));
console.log("password_len", (p || "").length);
console.log("password_equals_envfile", p === "EnvFileOnlySecret");

With the project .env renamed away so only secrets.env could supply the password:

$ docker compose -f compose.better.yml run --rm --no-deps app
password_in_process_env true
password_len 17
NODE_ENV production
password_equals_envfile true
password_equals_host_dotenv false

password_len 17 matches EnvFileOnlySecret. The host-interpolated value never appeared.

The ${} gotcha inside command: strings

I put a JS template literal in the Compose command once. Compose warned and emptied it:

level=warning msg="The \"t\" variable is not set. Defaulting to a blank string."

Resolved command became console.log('template', \token=); with no t. The container never saw ${t}. Fix: move the script to a file (as above), or escape as $$t in the YAML so Compose emits a literal $t for the shell or Node source.

Failure checklist

  1. .gitignore after the first commit. Tracked paths ignore the ignore file. Run git ls-files .env and git check-ignore -v .env.
  2. git rm --cached without rotating. Future commits are clean. Clones of the old history still have the password.
  3. .env.example missing or filled with real values. People copy the wrong file. Keep fake placeholders only.
  4. Mode 644 on the VPS secrets file. Any local account can read it. Use 600.
  5. ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} in Compose YAML. docker compose config prints the value. Prefer env_file and build URLs inside the app from separate env vars.
  6. JS ${...} inside Compose command:. Compose eats it. Use a file or $$.
  7. Assuming a private GitHub repo is enough. Private today can be public tomorrow, or the laptop backup can leak. History still carries the blob.
  8. Committing secrets.env "just for the team". That is the same bug with a different filename. Use a password manager, sealed secrets, or a one-time scp onto the VPS.

Where this shows up for me

The stack I'm building, Epure, is a two-container Compose file (Rust binary + Postgres 16) for exception-only error monitoring. Same rule as above: example env in git, real DSN and DB password only on the host. The product is not APM, replay, or logs. If you self-host it, the docs assume you already keep secrets out of the repo.

After you stop tracking .env, do you rotate the leaked secret, or only fix the ignore file?

articles.title: Doom Ran Inside TypeScript's Type Checker. Here's How Types Execute Code
articles.description: Doom's first frame took 12 days of type checking. The machinery: recursive conditional types, tuple-length math, and the limits tsc enforces.
articles.body_html:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The first frame of Doom took 12 days to render. None of the game's code ran as JavaScript. The TypeScript type checker evaluated it, at about 20 million type instantiations per second, until the frame came out the other end as a type.

That was February 2025. Dimitri Mitropoulos, founder of Michigan TypeScript, published a video showing Doom running on a WebAssembly virtual machine written entirely in TypeScript types. Simon Willison's write-up puts the scale at 177 TB of data, or about 3.5 trillion lines of type definitions. Socket's coverage adds that a typical TypeScript app might produce 200,000 to 500,000 type instantiations in total. Doom needed 20 million of them every second, for 12 days straight.

The stunt is absurd on purpose, but it runs on the same recursive conditional types, infer, and template literals you already use for route parsers and deep Partial helpers. You can build a small adder out of that machinery in a few lines, and the walls it hits are the ones Doom had to tear down.

What actually ran

Mitropoulos did not write Doom in types. He wrote a WebAssembly runtime in types, then fed it Doom compiled to WebAssembly. The runtime is public on GitHub and its README describes it as a WebAssembly runtime "implemented purely in TypeScript types": you give it a program, the type checker evaluates it, and the result is a type.

According to Socket, the runtime implements the 116 WebAssembly instructions Doom needs, and the type checker executed about 18 million instructions, one at a time, to draw the first frame. To do it, the VM simulates RAM, a call stack, memory pointers, and an execution context, along with a type-level garbage collector and an L1 cache. Numbers live as binary two's complement digits inside string literal types.

The same article reports that the project needed up to 100 GB of memory, and that the first estimate for one frame was 1.25 petabytes of types over three months, before optimizations cut it to 177 TB in 12 days.


The type checker as a machine: types go in, a type comes out.

Conditional types are a loop with an exit

Every type-level program is built from one primitive: a conditional type that refers to itself.

type Last<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;

type TrimLeft<S extends string> =
  S extends ` ${infer Rest}` ? TrimLeft<Rest> : S;

type A = Last<[1, 2, 3]>;      // 3
type B = TrimLeft<"   hi">;   // "hi"

T extends X ? Yes : No is your if. infer is pattern matching that binds a variable. Referring to the alias inside its own branch is recursion. That is enough to compute anything a machine can, given unlimited time and memory, and tsc gives you neither.

TrimLeft is the example the TypeScript 4.5 release notes use, and it comes with a warning: before 4.5, a string with 50 leading spaces was enough to trigger "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite."

Counting with tuple lengths

Types have no +. They do have tuples, and a tuple's length is a number literal type. So you count by building tuples.

type BuildTuple<
  N extends number,
  T extends unknown[] = [],
> = T["length"] extends N ? T : BuildTuple<N, [...T, unknown]>;

type Add<A extends number, B extends number> =
  [...BuildTuple<A>, ...BuildTuple<B>]["length"];

type Five = Add<2, 3>; // 5

BuildTuple<3> keeps appending unknown until the tuple's length equals 3. Add spreads two of those tuples into one and reads the length back out. Subtraction is the same trick in reverse: match [...BuildTuple<B>, ...infer Rest] and take the length of Rest.

The Doom runtime uses this exact move at its core. Its add.ts turns each binary digit into a tuple of zero or one element, spreads the two digits plus the carry into a single tuple, and reads the length (0 to 3) to decide the output digit and the next carry. Tuple length is the adder.

The three walls: 100 deep, 1,000 long, 5 million total

Now try Add<1500, 1>. It should fail, and the way it fails tells you which limit you hit.

tsc enforces three separate limits. Each one exists so a bad type cannot hang your editor:

  1. Instantiation depth: 100. Nested instantiations, where evaluating one type requires evaluating another inside it, stop at a depth of 100. PR #45711 set this in TypeScript 4.5. The old value was 50; an earlier change had raised it to 500, and users hit stack overflows.
  2. Tail-recursive iterations: 1,000. The same PR made tsc evaluate a conditional type whose branch is another conditional type in a loop instead of on the call stack. That loop gives up after 1,000 iterations.
  3. Instantiation count: 5 million. A running total of instantiations per checked expression or statement. Herrington Darkholme's walk through the checker source quotes the check as instantiationDepth === 100 || instantiationCount >= 5000000, alongside the tailCount === 1000 check for the loop.

BuildTuple is written in tail position: when it recurses, it returns the recursive result directly and does nothing else with it. That puts it in the 1,000-iteration loop instead of the 100-deep stack. Add<600, 700> should resolve to 1300, because each BuildTuple call stays under 1,000 iterations even though the final tuple is longer. Add<1500, 1> asks one BuildTuple for 1,500 iterations and runs into the cap.

Now break the tail position on purpose:

type Count<
  N extends number,
  T extends unknown[] = [],
> = T["length"] extends N
  ? []
  : [unknown, ...Count<N, [...T, unknown]>];

Count<N> also produces a tuple of length N, but it wraps the recursive call in a spread, so each step has to wait for the next one to finish. That is the non-tail shape the 4.5 release notes say won't be optimized. It runs against the depth limit instead of the iteration limit, and it gives up far sooner than BuildTuple does. The fix is the one the release notes give for their GetChars example: move the work into an accumulator parameter so the recursive call is the whole branch.

I haven't run these snippets for this post. Paste them into the TypeScript Playground and hover the aliases to see where your version of the compiler draws the line.


Three different limits stop three different kinds of recursion.

Doom does not fit under any of these walls. Socket reports that Mitropoulos temporarily patched the compiler during development to remove the safeguards: the type-instantiation depth limit, the recursion limits, the stack depth limit when comparing types, and the maximum size of unions and tuples, which he set to infinity. You will not get that build from npm. The Go-based compiler behind TypeScript 7 keeps these limits too. When someone asked in September 2026 whether they would be revisited for the new compiler, a maintainer answered: "We have no plans to change these limits."

Arithmetic on string literals

Tuple counting does not scale to 32-bit numbers. You cannot build a tuple of four billion elements. So the Doom runtime stores each number as a string of bits and does arithmetic one character at a time, like the adder circuit in a CPU.

Here is a small version. Bits are little-endian, least significant first, so the carry flows in the same direction tsc reads the string:

type Sum<A extends string, B extends string, C extends string> =
  `${A}${B}${C}` extends "000" ? ["0", "0"]
  : `${A}${B}${C}` extends "001" | "010" | "100" ? ["1", "0"]
  : `${A}${B}${C}` extends "011" | "101" | "110" ? ["0", "1"]
  : ["1", "1"];

type AddBits<
  A extends string,
  B extends string,
  C extends string = "0",
  Out extends string = "",
> = A extends `${infer a}${infer RestA}`
  ? B extends `${infer b}${infer RestB}`
    ? Sum<a, b, C> extends [
        infer D extends string,
        infer K extends string,
      ]
      ? AddBits<RestA, RestB, K, `${Out}${D}`>
      : never
    : never
  : C extends "1" ? `${Out}1` : Out;

// 3 + 1: "11" + "10" little-endian is "001", which is 4
type Four = AddBits<"11", "10">;

Sum is a one-bit full adder written as a lookup: three input bits, one output digit, one carry. AddBits peels the first character off each input with infer, adds them, appends the digit to Out, and recurses with the new carry. The recursive call sits at the end of a chain of conditional branches, so it is the shape PR #45711 evaluates in a loop. A 32-bit add takes about a hundred loop steps (three conditionals per bit), still well inside 1,000. The inputs must have the same length; the real runtime handles uneven inputs and pads to fixed widths.

The little-endian order matters. Template literal patterns match from the left, and ${infer a}${infer Rest} grabs the first character cheaply. Taking the last character means walking the whole string. Socket notes that because TypeScript only iterates strings from the left, Mitropoulos wrote all the binary algorithms in reverse. His add.ts reverses both inputs, adds, and reverses the result back, and a comment in the file calls that reversal a major recursion bottleneck.

Multiply, divide, and shift can follow the same pattern: a per-bit table plus a tail-recursive walk. Stack 116 of those instructions on a state machine that tracks memory and a program counter, and you have a CPU that runs in the checker.

What this means for the types you ship

You will never put Doom in your codebase. You will write a route parser, a typed SQL builder, a deep Paths<T> helper, or a schema-to-type mapper, and those run on the same machinery with the same three walls.

Keep recursion in tail position. If a recursive call is wrapped in a union, a spread, or an object, add an accumulator parameter and return the call bare. That moves your type from the 100-deep wall to the 1,000-iteration one.

Know which wall you hit. "Excessively deep and possibly infinite" is TS2589, and it can come from depth, from the iteration cap, or from the 5 million total. The fix differs: depth wants tail calls, the iteration cap wants shorter inputs or chunking, and the total wants fewer distributive unions in the hot path.

Next time TS2589 shows up in a helper you wrote, run tsc --extendedDiagnostics before you blame the IDE. It prints where the compiler spends its time and how many types it creates, which is your first clue to which of the three counters you blew.

If this was useful

Recursive conditional types, infer, template literal parsing, and the accumulator pattern that keeps you under the recursion limits are the core of The TypeScript Type System, book 2 in The TypeScript Library. If the AddBits walk made sense but you would not trust yourself to write the next one, that book takes you from generics to DSL-level types one step at a time.

The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection. Books 1 and 2 are the core path; 3 and 4 substitute for 1 and 2 if you come from the JVM or PHP; book 5 is for anyone shipping TS at work.

  1. TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling across Node, Bun, Deno, and the browser.
  2. The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types.
  3. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — variance, null safety, sealed classes to unions, coroutines to async/await.
  4. PHP to TypeScript — the sync-to-async shift, generics, discriminated unions for PHP 8+ developers.
  5. TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.
